options.B: Managing hospital finances and paying medical bills directly
options.C: Prescribing antidepressant medications during ward rounds
options.D: Coordinating services and keeping the patient central to the plan

explanation: The nurse acts as the central coordinator, bridging communication between various specialists and advocating for the patient's needs. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T4#GNS311_U2_T4_h8)

question: What is the main goal of blood and bone marrow tests?

options.A: To treat infectious diseases like malaria
options.B: To find blood and bone marrow disorders
options.C: To measure kidney function and body salts
options.D: To check the heart's electrical activity

explanation: Haematological tests specifically look at blood components and bone marrow to catch disorders early. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why is a careful diagnostic step important in Nigerian hospitals when checking blood?

options.A: It replaces the need for physical checks
options.B: It stops wrong diagnoses when common infections mimic blood issues
options.C: It means the patient goes home the same day
options.D: It removes the need for expensive genetic tests

explanation: Common endemic infections can look like blood disorders, so careful testing helps nurses and doctors avoid mistakes. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h1)

question: Yellow eyes and skin (jaundice) during a physical check usually points to what?

options.A: A bacterial infection in the lymph glands
options.B: Haemolytic anaemia from red blood cells breaking down
options.C: Low iron from long-term blood loss
options.D: Low overall bone marrow production

explanation: When red blood cells break down too fast, they release bilirubin, which causes yellowing of the eyes and skin. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h2)

question: A patient has painless neck lumps and feels tired all the time. What is this clinical sign called?

options.A: Splenomegaly
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Lymphadenopathy
options.D: Pallor

explanation: Enlarged lymph nodes are charted as lymphadenopathy, which often shows up with infections or certain diseases. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h2)

question: Which test result helps sort different types of anaemia by the size of the red blood cells?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: White blood cell count
options.C: Mean Corpuscular Volume
options.D: Platelet count

explanation: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) tells you the average size of red blood cells, grouping anaemias into small, normal, or large cell types. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the big advantage of looking at a blood smear under a microscope compared to a standard automated blood count?

options.A: It gives a faster printout of total platelets
options.B: It lets you directly see the shape and structure of blood cells
options.C: It checks chemical salts inside the plasma
options.D: It replaces a bone marrow test completely

explanation: A microscope lets lab scientists and clinicians spot unusual cell shapes, like sickled cells or abnormal blasts, that machine counters might miss. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h3)

question: Where is the safest and most common spot to take a bone marrow sample in an adult?

options.A: The middle of the shin bone
options.B: The front part of the shoulder bone
options.C: The breastbone
options.D: The back part of the hip bone (posterior iliac spine)

explanation: The posterior superior iliac spine is the preferred site because it is safe and avoids major internal organs. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why do doctors often take a bone marrow biopsy core right along with a fluid aspiration?

options.A: To check clotting proteins in the blood
options.B: To flush out bad fluid from the bone
options.C: To check the structure and overall space inside the bone marrow
options.D: To measure oxygen levels in arteries

explanation: While fluid aspiration shows the individual cells, a solid biopsy piece shows how the bone marrow is built and packed inside. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which blood test is mostly used to check patients taking oral warfarin?

options.A: Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time
options.B: Complete blood cell count
options.C: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.D: Prothrombin Time and INR

explanation: Prothrombin Time and the International Normalized Ratio (INR) track the clotting pathway that warfarin affects. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h5)

question: The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) test is used to monitor treatment with which drug?

options.A: Warfarin
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Heparin
options.D: Aspirin

explanation: aPTT measures the intrinsic clotting pathway, making it the standard test for managing heparin therapy. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which test is the gold standard for confirming sickle cell disease types?

options.A: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
options.B: Activated partial thromboplastin time
options.C: Bone marrow core biopsy
options.D: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate

explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis separates different types of haemoglobin using an electrical charge, clearly showing sickle cell variants. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the main job of flow cytometry in blood tests?

options.A: To screen for inherited bleeding disorders
options.B: To count the percentage of red blood cells
options.C: To measure how thick whole blood is
options.D: To spot specific markers on cells to help classify blood cancers like leukemia

explanation: Flow cytometry uses lasers and antibodies to detect special markers on cell surfaces, helping diagnose types of leukemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h6)

question: What typical bone change shows up on a plain X-ray for a patient with multiple myeloma?

options.A: Narrowing of the spinal canal
options.B: An enlarged spleen
options.C: Lytic bone lesions (punched-out spots)
options.D: Widespread hairline bone cracks

explanation: Multiple myeloma causes areas of bone breakdown that look like little punched-out holes on standard X-rays. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why do doctors order a CT scan for a patient with lymphoma?

options.A: To check for swollen lymph nodes in the chest, belly, and pelvis
options.B: To measure the exact haemoglobin amount in blood
options.C: To see tiny cell markers on white blood cells
options.D: To check the heart's electrical pathways

explanation: CT scans give cross-sectional pictures that help stage lymphoma by revealing the size and spread of lymph nodes inside the body cavities. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is an important nursing duty right after a patient has a bone marrow biopsy?

options.A: Tell the patient to walk around the ward immediately
options.B: Give blood thinners so clots don't form
options.C: Check vital signs and watch the biopsy site for bleeding
options.D: Put a hot water bottle right on the puncture site

explanation: After the procedure, the nurse's main focus is watching for early bleeding and making sure the patient's vitals stay stable. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h8)

question: Why is labeling blood and bone marrow samples correctly so critical?

options.A: It makes lab machines run faster
options.B: It lowers the cost of genetic testing
options.C: It means nurses don't have to write in the patient chart
options.D: It prevents dangerous mistakes with wrong diagnoses and treatments

explanation: A mislabeled sample can lead to the wrong diagnosis, mismatched blood transfusions, and serious harm to the patient. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T5#GNS311_U2_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological defect in anaemia?

options.A: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood
options.B: Increased white blood cell destruction rate
options.C: Decreased overall body fluid volume
options.D: Elevated plasma volume without cells

explanation: Anaemia fundamentally reduces the blood's ability to transport sufficient oxygen to body tissues due to low haemoglobin or red cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h1)

question: The kidneys respond to systemic tissue hypoxia by releasing which specific hormone?

options.A: Erythropoietin
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Aldosterone
options.D: Vasopressin

explanation: Hypoxia in renal tissues stimulates the release of erythropoietin to signal the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h1)

question: Iron deficiency anaemia is classically classified under which morphological group?

options.A: Microcytic hypochromic
options.B: Macrocytic normochromic
options.C: Microcytic hyperchromic
options.D: Normocytic megaloblastic

explanation: A shortage of iron impairs haemoglobin synthesis, yielding smaller and paler red blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h2)

question: A patient diagnosed with vitamin B12 deficiency will most likely present with what type of red blood cells?

options.A: Microcytic
options.B: Spherocytic
options.C: Normocytic
options.D: Macrocytic

explanation: Impaired DNA synthesis from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency prevents proper cell division, resulting in abnormally large cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h2)

question: Which physical assessment finding is most characteristic of chronic iron deficiency anaemia?

options.A: Moon face
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Koilonychia
options.D: Trismus

explanation: Spoon-shaped nails, known as koilonychia, are a classic physical sign associated with long-standing iron deficiency. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why do patients with moderate anaemia frequently complain of palpitations and fatigue?

options.A: Low blood pressure directly damages peripheral nerve endings
options.B: Metabolic waste products accumulate rapidly in the bloodstream
options.C: Excess red blood cells block small capillaries in muscles
options.D: The heart works harder to deliver enough oxygen to tissues

explanation: Cardiovascular compensation increases heart rate to maintain tissue oxygenation, causing palpitations and generalized exhaustion. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which laboratory test gives the most accurate measure of total body iron stores?

options.A: Serum potassium
options.B: Serum ferritin
options.C: Total leukocyte count
options.D: Prothrombin time

explanation: Ferritin is the primary storage protein for iron, making its serum level a direct indicator of body iron reserves. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h4)

question: A patient with suspected chronic gastrointestinal bleeding should have which diagnostic investigation ordered first?

options.A: Sputum microscopy
options.B: Liver function test
options.C: Electrocardiogram
options.D: Stool occult blood test

explanation: Checking stool for hidden blood helps identify occult gastrointestinal bleeding as a potential underlying cause of blood loss anaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the standard first-line pharmacological treatment for uncomplicated iron deficiency anaemia?

options.A: Subcutaneous erythropoietin
options.B: Intravenous folic acid
options.C: Oral ferrous sulfate
options.D: Intramuscular vitamin B12

explanation: Oral iron salts are the most accessible and cost-effective first-line treatment for replacing depleted iron stores. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h5)

question: When is a blood transfusion typically prioritized over oral supplements in managing anaemia?

options.A: When the patient has severe symptoms and dangerously low haemoglobin
options.B: Whenever the patient prefers a rapid recovery before discharge
options.C: Only when oral iron therapy causes mild gastrointestinal upset
options.D: As a routine replacement for patients with chronic mild fatigue

explanation: Transfusions carry risks and are reserved for acute, severe drops in haemoglobin where oxygen delivery is critically compromised. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h5)

question: A patient taking oral iron supplements should be advised to take them with what substance to improve absorption?

options.A: Fresh milk
options.B: Black coffee
options.C: Antacid syrup
options.D: Orange juice

explanation: Vitamin C in citrus juice creates an acidic environment that enhances the gastrointestinal absorption of iron. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for scheduling frequent rest periods for a hospitalized anaemic patient?

options.A: To allow routine blood pressure checks without interruption
options.B: To reduce myocardial oxygen demand and conserve patient energy
options.C: To prevent the oral iron medication from causing sudden nausea
options.D: To encourage faster elimination of metabolic waste products

explanation: Anaemic hearts already work harder to pump blood; resting prevents overexertion and reduces cardiac workload. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h6)

question: Long-standing severe anaemia can lead to which major cardiac complication?

options.A: High-output heart failure
options.B: Chronic rheumatic carditis
options.C: Constrictive pericarditis
options.D: Primary pulmonary hypertension

explanation: The chronic demand for increased cardiac output eventually exhausts the myocardium, resulting in heart failure. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a suitable dietary recommendation for managing iron deficiency anaemia?

options.A: Drinking large quantities of strong tea with meals
options.B: Eating lean red meat when available
options.C: Consuming dark green leafy vegetables regularly
options.D: Including beans and legumes in daily diets

explanation: Tannins in tea bind to iron in the digestive tract and significantly inhibit its absorption, making it an unsuitable recommendation. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T6#GNS311_U2_T6_h7)

question: What structural change occurs in the haemoglobin molecule during sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Oxygen molecules destroy the beta chain
options.B: Glutamic acid is replaced by valine
options.C: Valine is replaced by iron molecules
options.D: Lysine is substituted for normal plasma

explanation: A point mutation alters the beta-globin chain by replacing glutamic acid with valine. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why do red blood cells take on a rigid, sickle shape in this condition?

options.A: Excess dietary iron crystallises inside the cell membrane
options.B: Deoxygenated haemoglobin S forms rigid polymers
options.C: White blood cells attack the circulating erythrocytes
options.D: Plasma proteins coat the cell and cause dehydration

explanation: Low oxygen levels cause abnormal haemoglobin S to stick together into stiff fibres that distort the cell. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h1)

question: What is the term for painful swelling of the hands and feet in infants with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Dactylitis
options.B: Osteomyelitis
options.C: Vaso-occlusion
options.D: Splenomegaly

explanation: Hand-foot syndrome, or dactylitis, is an early sign of blocked blood flow in small bones. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h2)

question: A young patient with sickle cell anaemia presents with painful, swollen fingers. What process is happening?

options.A: Excessive accumulation of white blood cells
options.B: Rapid destruction of platelets in the marrow
options.C: Bacterial invasion of the joint capsule
options.D: Microvascular occlusion in the small bones

explanation: Sickled cells block tiny blood vessels in the hands and feet, causing ischemia and swelling. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h2)

question: Which laboratory test is considered the definitive confirmatory method for diagnosing sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: Complete blood count
options.C: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
options.D: Routine clotting profile

explanation: Electrophoresis separates haemoglobin variants to confirm the presence of HbS. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why does a peripheral blood smear show Howell-Jolly bodies in a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Red blood cells are dividing too rapidly
options.B: Bone marrow is producing excess white blood cells
options.C: Platelets are clumping together in large numbers
options.D: The spleen has lost its filtering function

explanation: Functional asplenia prevents the spleen from removing nuclear remnants from red blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why is monitoring body temperature particularly critical in a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Warmth increases the effectiveness of prescribed oral iron supplements
options.B: Fever confirms the exact onset of a painful vaso-occlusive crisis
options.C: Fever often indicates a life-threatening infection due to asplenia
options.D: Elevated temperature directly triggers immediate massive red blood cell sickling

explanation: Splenic dysfunction increases vulnerability to encapsulated organisms, making fever a medical emergency. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h4)

question: A nurse notices a drop in oxygen saturation and new chest pain in a hospitalised sickle cell patient. What complication is suspected?

options.A: Acute chest syndrome
options.B: Splenic sequestration
options.C: Aplastic crisis
options.D: Biliary colic

explanation: New respiratory symptoms and chest infiltrates point toward acute chest syndrome, a pulmonary emergency. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the primary physiological goal of administering intravenous fluids during a painful crisis?

options.A: To prevent the kidneys from absorbing excess iron
options.B: To dilute circulating white blood cells and stop inflammation
options.C: To increase total red blood cell production rapidly
options.D: To reduce blood viscosity and improve microvascular flow

explanation: Hydration thins the blood, helping the compromised erythrocytes pass through narrow vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which intervention should be avoided or used with caution during routine management of a vaso-occlusive crisis?

options.A: Aggressive intravenous rehydration with isotonic saline solutions
options.B: Scheduled administration of prescribed opioid pain medications
options.C: Prompt identification and treatment of underlying infections
options.D: Routine administration of high-flow oxygen without hypoxia

explanation: Oxygen is only needed if oxygen saturation is low, as it does not reverse polymerisation without hypoxia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h5)

question: How does hydroxyurea benefit patients with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: It directly dissolves existing intravascular blood clots
options.B: It increases the production of foetal haemoglobin
options.C: It destroys defective white blood cells in the marrow
options.D: It permanently removes abnormal iron stores from the liver

explanation: Foetal haemoglobin prevents the polymerization of haemoglobin S, reducing sickling episodes. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why is long-term blood transfusion therapy often paired with iron chelation agents?

options.A: To prevent dangerous accumulation of excess iron in body tissues
options.B: To block the immune system from attacking donated cells
options.C: To stimulate the bone marrow to produce normal adult cells
options.D: To enhance the effectiveness of red blood cell destruction

explanation: Repeated blood transfusions dump excess iron into the body, which can damage organs without chelation. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h6)

question: What happens during a splenic sequestration crisis?

options.A: Bone marrow halts all red blood cell production abruptly
options.B: Infection destroys the splenic capsule and causes peritonitis
options.C: Blood pools massively within the spleen, causing shock
options.D: The spleen stops filtering white blood cells completely

explanation: Trapped blood in the spleen leads to sudden organ enlargement and severe hypovolaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h7)

question: Which preventive measure is essential for children with sickle cell anaemia to reduce infection risks?

options.A: Monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions
options.B: Daily supplementation with high-dose vitamin C
options.C: Avoidance of all physical exercise and sports
options.D: Prophylactic daily oral penicillin administration

explanation: Daily penicillin protects against severe pneumococcal infections caused by impaired splenic function. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h7)

question: What advice should a nurse give a family regarding travel to high-altitude mountainous regions?

options.A: Avoid high altitudes because low oxygen pressure can trigger a crisis
options.B: High altitudes help stimulate the production of healthy blood cells
options.C: Only children under five years old are affected by thin air
options.D: Travel is completely safe as long as fluid intake is doubled

explanation: Reduced atmospheric oxygen at high altitudes can precipitate red blood cell sickling and hypoxia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h8)

question: Why is genetic counselling recommended for individuals with sickle cell trait or disease?

options.A: To diagnose acute complications before physical symptoms appear
options.B: To monitor laboratory values related to chronic iron overload
options.C: To explain inheritance risks and assist with family planning decisions
options.D: To prescribe the correct daily doses of prophylactic antibiotics

explanation: Counselling helps families understand how the autosomal recessive trait is passed to offspring. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T7#GNS311_U2_T7_h8)

question: What primary blood component is increased in patients with polycythaemia?

options.A: Red blood cells
options.B: Blood platelets
options.C: White blood cells
options.D: Blood plasma

explanation: Polycythaemia specifically refers to an abnormal elevation in the volume of circulating red blood cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h1)

question: How does an elevated red blood cell count directly affect blood circulation?

options.A: It reduces blood pressure in major arteries
options.B: It increases blood viscosity and slows down flow
options.C: It thins the plasma to prevent vessel blockage
options.D: It accelerates oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues

explanation: Higher red blood cell mass thickens the blood, raising viscosity and impairing smooth microvascular flow. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which condition is classified as a primary type of polycythaemia?

options.A: Chronic lung disease
options.B: Renal cell carcinoma
options.C: Polycythaemia vera
options.D: High altitude hypoxia

explanation: Polycythaemia vera arises from intrinsic bone marrow stem cell mutations, making it a primary disorder. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h2)

question: Secondary polycythaemia is most commonly triggered by an increase in which substance?

options.A: Blood platelets
options.B: Erythropoietin
options.C: Serum albumin
options.D: Thrombopoietin

explanation: Extrinsic factors causing secondary polycythaemia typically stimulate the kidneys to release excess erythropoietin. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h2)

question: The JAK2 genetic mutation is strongly linked to which type of polycythaemia?

options.A: Primary polycythaemia
options.B: Secondary polycythaemia
options.C: Relative polycythaemia
options.D: Dehydration polycythaemia

explanation: Acquired mutations in the JAK2 gene are the hallmark genetic driver of primary polycythaemia vera. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h3)

question: A patient with chronic lung disease develops secondary polycythaemia due to which underlying process?

options.A: Direct bone marrow stimulation by nicotine
options.B: Autoimmune destruction of blood vessels
options.C: Rapid proliferation of white blood cells
options.D: Persistent systemic tissue hypoxia

explanation: Chronic lung disease limits oxygen exchange, causing low oxygen levels that prompt the kidneys to produce more erythropoietin. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h3)

question: Which skin finding is most characteristic of a patient with polycythaemia?

options.A: Diffuse skin pallor
options.B: Cyanotic nail beds
options.C: Generalized jaundice
options.D: Ruddy facial plethora

explanation: The high concentration of haemoglobin gives the skin and mucous membranes a flushed, ruddy appearance. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why do patients with polycythaemia often experience intense itching after a warm bath?

options.A: Histamine release from activated basophils
options.B: Severe dryness of the skin epidermis
options.C: Allergic reaction to bath soap chemicals
options.D: Dilation of superficial dermal lymphatics

explanation: Warm water triggers the release of histamine and other pruritogens from circulating blood cells, causing aquagenic pruritus. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h4)

question: Serum erythropoietin levels are typically found to be what in patients with polycythaemia vera?

options.A: Extremely high
options.B: Significantly low
options.C: Fluctuating daily
options.D: Normal range

explanation: In polycythaemia vera, autonomous red blood cell production suppresses natural erythropoietin output by the kidneys. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of genetic testing for the JAK2 mutation in this context?

options.A: To confirm a diagnosis of primary polycythaemia
options.B: To determine the degree of chronic lung impairment
options.C: To measure the exact volume of circulating plasma
options.D: To evaluate the risk of acute bacterial infection

explanation: The JAK2 mutation marker is diagnostic for primary myeloproliferative neoplasms like polycythaemia vera. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary objective of performing therapeutic phlebotomy in polycythaemia?

options.A: To lower blood viscosity and haematocrit
options.B: To increase total serum iron stores
options.C: To stimulate new white blood cell growth
options.D: To correct chronic respiratory acidosis

explanation: Phlebotomy reduces red cell mass, directly decreasing blood thickness and preventing sluggish flow. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h6)

question: A patient undergoing treatment for polycythaemia is prescribed low-dose aspirin primarily to prevent which complication?

options.A: Bone marrow failure
options.B: Splenic rupture
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Thrombus formation

explanation: Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin helps prevent the blood clots that commonly occur due to hyperviscosity. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h6)

question: Which serious vascular event is most commonly associated with untreated polycythaemia?

options.A: Valvular stenosis
options.B: Thrombosis
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Aortic aneurysm

explanation: Sluggish, viscous blood significantly increases the likelihood of abnormal clot formation in arteries and veins. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is a recognized long-term risk of primary polycythaemia vera over many years?

options.A: Permanent structural heart valve damage
options.B: Transformation to acute leukaemia
options.C: Complete recovery of bone marrow function
options.D: Development of chronic kidney failure

explanation: Polycythaemia vera carries a long-term risk of evolving into myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukaemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T8#GNS311_U2_T8_h7)

question: What is the primary function of the lymphatic system's white blood cells?

options.A: Carrying oxygen
options.B: Digesting fats
options.C: Fighting infection
options.D: Clotting blood

explanation: Lymphocytes are specialized white blood cells responsible for defending the body against pathogens and infections. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h1)

question: How do lymphomas develop within the lymphatic system?

options.A: Bone marrow fails to release mature platelets
options.B: Lymphocytes multiply uncontrollably and become malignant
options.C: Lymph vessels become blocked by excess fluid
options.D: The spleen stops producing red blood cells

explanation: Lymphomas start when normal lymphocytes undergo malignant changes and multiply without typical regulatory control. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h1)

question: Which specific cell type is diagnostic for Hodgkin Lymphoma?

options.A: Plasma cells
options.B: Kupffer cells
options.C: Reed-Sternberg cells
options.D: Epithelioid cells

explanation: The presence of giant, abnormal Reed-Sternberg cells is the hallmark diagnostic feature of Hodgkin Lymphoma. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h2)

question: What pattern of spread typically distinguishes Hodgkin Lymphoma from Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma?

options.A: Immediate destruction of circulating red blood cells
options.B: Predictable spread to adjacent lymph node groups
options.C: Rapid spread exclusively to the central nervous system
options.D: Random involvement of distant skin tissues only

explanation: Hodgkin Lymphoma characteristically spreads in an orderly, contiguous fashion from one lymph node chain to the next. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which viral infection is strongly associated with endemic Burkitt lymphoma in Nigeria?

options.A: Cytomegalovirus
options.B: Herpes simplex virus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Hepatitis B virus

explanation: Epstein-Barr virus plays a major role in the pathogenesis of endemic Burkitt lymphoma found frequently in children in sub-Saharan Africa. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h3)

question: Why do many lymphoma patients in Nigeria often present late to healthcare facilities?

options.A: Routine annual physical examinations in rural areas
options.B: Strict government policies on mandatory screening
options.C: Immediate access to advanced molecular testing
options.D: Misdiagnosis as infectious diseases and financial barriers

explanation: Poverty, diagnostic delays, and initial confusion with common conditions like tuberculosis often delay definitive lymphoma treatment in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h3)

question: What type of lymph node enlargement is most characteristic of early lymphoma?

options.A: Warm and erythematous
options.B: Hard and fixed to skin
options.C: Painless and rubbery
options.D: Painful and fluctuant

explanation: Enlarged lymph nodes in lymphoma are typically firm, rubbery to the touch, and remarkably painless. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h4)

question: Which clinical findings constitute the classic 'B symptoms' in lymphoma patients?

options.A: Fever, night sweats, and weight loss
options.B: Jaundice, pruritus, and joint swelling
options.C: Headache, dizziness, and blurred vision
options.D: Hypertension, edema, and proteinuria

explanation: B symptoms refer specifically to unexplained fevers, drenching night sweats, and significant unintentional weight loss. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the gold standard diagnostic procedure for confirming a diagnosis of lymphoma?

options.A: Excisional lymph node biopsy
options.B: Complete blood count with differential
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.D: Peripheral blood smear examination

explanation: Examining an excised lymph node under a microscope provides the necessary tissue architecture to definitively diagnose lymphoma. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h5)

question: What does Stage IV classification indicate in the Ann Arbor staging system for lymphomas?

options.A: Disease limited to lymph nodes above the diaphragm
options.B: Primary tumor located strictly within the bone marrow
options.C: Involvement of a single lymph node region only
options.D: Widespread involvement of extra-lymphatic organs

explanation: Stage IV represents disseminated disease with multiple or diffuse involvement of extra-lymphatic organs like the liver or bone marrow. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h5)

question: What class of medication is Rituximab, commonly used in Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma treatment?

options.A: Monoclonal antibody
options.B: Antifungal antibiotic
options.C: Loop diuretic
options.D: Alkylating agent

explanation: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody targeted against the CD20 antigen found on the surface of B-cells. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h6)

question: Why are multi-agent chemotherapy regimens preferred over single-agent therapy in lymphoma management?

options.A: They completely eliminate the risk of systemic side effects for patients
options.B: They shorten the required treatment duration to a single hospital visit
options.C: They attack cancer cells through different mechanisms and reduce drug resistance
options.D: They prevent the need for any supportive laboratory monitoring

explanation: Using multiple drugs with distinct mechanisms of action maximizes tumor cell destruction while minimizing drug resistance. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h6)

question: What primary risk does chemotherapy-induced bone marrow suppression pose to lymphoma patients?

options.A: Hypertension and edema
options.B: Infection and bleeding
options.C: Hyperglycemia and seizures
options.D: Bone demineralization

explanation: Suppression of bone marrow leads to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, increasing vulnerability to severe infections and bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h7)

question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy for lymphoma develops painful oral ulcers. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

options.A: Restrict fluid intake to keep the oral cavity dry
options.B: Scrub the oral mucosa firmly with a hard toothbrush
options.C: Recommend highly spiced foods to stimulate appetite
options.D: Encourage gentle mouth rinses with normal saline

explanation: Saline mouth rinses soothe inflamed mucosal tissues and promote healing without causing further trauma or irritation. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h7)

question: What electrolyte imbalance is a hallmark feature of Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Hyperkalemia
options.B: Hyponatremia
options.C: Hypokalemia
options.D: Hypernatremia

explanation: The rapid lysis of massive numbers of tumor cells releases large amounts of intracellular potassium into the circulation, causing hyperkalemia. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h8)

question: Which clinical sign is most characteristic of Superior Vena Cava Syndrome in lymphoma?

options.A: Unilateral lower limb edema
options.B: Severe intermittent claudication
options.C: Facial and neck swelling
options.D: Pruritic generalized skin rash

explanation: Obstruction of blood flow through the superior vena cava causes congestion and visible swelling in the face, neck, and upper chest. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of palliative care in lymphoma management?

options.A: Replacing all forms of standard chemotherapy treatments
options.B: Accelerating the patient discharge process from hospital
options.C: Improving quality of life and relieving symptom distress
options.D: Achieving a complete cure for advanced malignancies

explanation: Palliative care focuses on symptom control, pain management, and enhancing the overall quality of life for patients and their families. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h9)

question: Why is patient education regarding infection prevention critical during lymphoma survivorship?

options.A: Patients are completely immune to viral infections forever
options.B: Nutritional supplements replace the need for hygiene practices
options.C: Immune function can remain compromised following treatments
options.D: Hospital readmissions are legally prohibited after discharge

explanation: Prior chemotherapy and radiation can leave lasting impacts on the immune system, requiring ongoing vigilance against infectious agents. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T9#GNS311_U2_T9_h9)

question: Which body part houses the organs for the special senses?

options.A: The torso
options.B: The limbs
options.C: The head
options.D: The skin

explanation: Special sense organs like the eyes, ears, and nose are all localized in the head region. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is sensory transduction?

options.A: Converting environmental stimuli into electrical signals
options.B: Filtering out pain signals
options.C: Producing chemical hormones
options.D: Amplifying weak sounds

explanation: Transduction is the translation of physical or chemical stimuli into electrical nerve impulses that the brain can understand. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which retinal photoreceptor cell is responsible for color vision?

options.A: Cones
options.B: Rods
options.C: Neurons
options.D: Cilia

explanation: Cone cells operate best in bright light and allow the perception of fine details and distinct colors. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h2)

question: A patient struggles to see in dim hospital corridors at night. Which retinal cells are likely underperforming?

options.A: Iris fibers
options.B: Rods
options.C: Cones
options.D: Corneal cells

explanation: Rods are specialized photoreceptors that function primarily in low-light environments for night and peripheral vision. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h2)

question: Name the three auditory ossicles found in the middle ear.

options.A: Sclera, choroid, and macula
options.B: Cornea, iris, and retina
options.C: Malleus, incus, and stapes
options.D: Cochlea, vestibule, and utricle

explanation: The middle ear contains three small interconnected bones—the malleus, incus, and stapes—that transmit sound vibrations. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h3)

question: Damage to the semicircular canals of the inner ear will most likely cause what symptom?

options.A: Total color blindness
options.B: Inability to taste sweet foods
options.C: Loss of balance and dizziness
options.D: Dryness of the nasal mucosa

explanation: The semicircular canals are part of the vestibular system responsible for detecting head movement and maintaining balance. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h3)

question: Where are the primary olfactory receptors located?

options.A: Inside the cochlea
options.B: On the cornea of the eye
options.C: Roof of the nasal cavity
options.D: Surface of the tongue

explanation: Olfactory receptors reside in the superior portion of the nasal cavity where they detect airborne chemical odorants. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h4)

question: Why does severe nasal congestion make food taste bland?

options.A: Saliva production completely stops
options.B: Cranial nerves are crushed by swelling
options.C: Olfactory input is blocked, reducing flavor perception
options.D: Taste buds are paralyzed by viruses

explanation: Much of what we perceive as taste relies on the sense of smell working in tandem with gustatory receptors. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which major brain structure acts as the relay station for almost all sensory pathways?

options.A: Thalamus
options.B: Medulla oblongata
options.C: Cerebellum
options.D: Pituitary gland

explanation: The thalamus processes and relays sensory signals to the appropriate regions of the cerebral cortex, with the sole exception of smell. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of sensory adaptation?

options.A: Enhancing night vision
options.B: Increasing pain sensitivity
options.C: Speeding up reflex arcs
options.D: Preventing sensory overload from constant stimuli

explanation: Sensory adaptation allows nerve receptors to slow down their firing when exposed to continuous, non-threatening stimuli. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h5)

question: What term describes the natural age-related hearing loss affecting high-frequency sounds?

options.A: Presbycusis
options.B: Anosmia
options.C: Presbyopia
options.D: Glaucoma

explanation: Presbycusis is the gradual, sensorineural hearing loss associated with aging, typically impacting higher frequencies first. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h6)

question: An elderly patient has decreased touch and temperature sensation. What is an important safety intervention?

options.A: Apply scented lotions every two hours
options.B: Turn off room lights completely
options.C: Check bathwater temperature with a thermometer
options.D: Restrict fluid intake at night

explanation: Patients with impaired touch and temperature senses are at high risk for accidental scald injuries, requiring nurse-verified water temperatures. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T1#GNS311_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the main goal of an initial EENT (Eye, Ear, Nose, and Throat) physical check?

options.A: To give broad antibiotics
options.B: To find localized pain and sensory changes
options.C: To test muscle strength
options.D: To schedule immediate surgery

explanation: Initial assessments focus on gathering patient history regarding pain, discharge, and changes in the eyes, ears, nose, or throat. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why do EENT exams require special lights and magnifying tools?

options.A: To measure nerve electricity
options.B: To replace health history taking
options.C: Because target areas are inside hidden cavities
options.D: So patients can see inside themselves

explanation: Specialized tools are essential for viewing hidden structures inside ear canals, nasal passages, and the throat. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which device measures fluid pressure inside the eye to check for glaucoma?

options.A: Ophthalmoscope
options.B: Tonometer
options.C: Spirometer
options.D: Otoscope

explanation: Tonometry measures eye pressure, which is vital for detecting and monitoring glaucoma. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of fluorescein angiography?

options.A: Testing peripheral vision fields
options.B: Determining eye pressure
options.C: Evaluating retinal blood vessels and leaks
options.D: Measuring cornea curvature

explanation: Fluorescein dye highlights blood vessels in the retina to help clinicians identify circulation problems or vessel leakage. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h2)

question: What does tympanometry measure during an ear evaluation?

options.A: High-frequency bone hearing in adults
options.B: Nerve impulses going to the brain
options.C: The angle of the ear canal
options.D: Middle ear movement and eardrum flexibility

explanation: Tympanometry assesses how well the middle ear transmits sound by changing air pressure in the ear canal. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h3)

question: What is the clinical use of the Rinne and Weber tuning fork tests?

options.A: Differentiating types of hearing loss
options.B: Evaluating the Eustachian tube
options.C: Checking balance centers
options.D: Measuring inner ear fluid pressure

explanation: Tuning fork tests provide a quick bedside method to determine whether hearing loss is due to nerve damage or sound conduction blockage. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h3)

question: What tool is commonly used to look deep into the nasal passages?

options.A: Blood pressure cuff
options.B: Ophthalmoscope lens
options.C: Fiberoptic nasal endoscope
options.D: Metallic ear speculum

explanation: Nasal endoscopes allow healthcare providers to see deep into nasal cavities and sinus openings that regular speculums cannot reach. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why are numbing sprays and decongestants used in the nose before an endoscopy?

options.A: To reduce swelling and patient discomfort
options.B: To kill bacterial infections
options.C: To widen the outer nose for lighting
options.D: To cause mucus production for lab tests

explanation: Decongestants shrink swollen nasal tissues to widen passages, while anesthetics numb the area to prevent pain. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why is a laryngeal mirror warmed before an indirect laryngoscopy?

options.A: To dilate throat blood vessels
options.B: To prevent fogging from breath moisture
options.C: To activate numbing spray faster
options.D: To sterilize the glass surface

explanation: Warming the mirror prevents condensation from blocking the view of the vocal cords during the exam. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the main goal of a flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES)?

options.A: Removing objects from the esophagus
options.B: Biopsying the soft palate
options.C: Observing swallowing during food consumption
options.D: Measuring air pressure in the trachea

explanation: FEES allows clinicians to watch how the throat handles food and liquids in real-time to detect aspiration risks. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which imaging study gives the best view of fine bone structures in the skull and sinuses?

options.A: Surface ultrasound
options.B: MRI scan
options.C: CT scan
options.D: Plain skull X-ray

explanation: CT scans offer exceptional detail for bony anatomy, making them the standard choice for evaluating sinuses and temporal bones. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h6)

question: When is an MRI preferred over a CT scan for EENT evaluations?

options.A: When the patient cannot lie flat
options.B: When detailed soft tissue and nerve pathways need viewing
options.C: When checking for metal objects
options.D: When checking for acute bone fractures after an accident

explanation: MRI excels at showing soft tissue details, such as the optic nerve or brain structures, without radiation exposure. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is a crucial nursing action after a patient receives throat numbing medication?

options.A: Placing the patient flat on their back for two hours
options.B: Withholding food and fluids until the gag reflex returns
options.C: Encouraging immediate oral liquid intake
options.D: Giving strong pain relievers

explanation: Topical anesthetics paralyze the throat temporarily, making patients prone to choking if they eat or drink before it wears off. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h7)

question: A patient scheduled for an EENT test is anxious and confused. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Proceed without mentioning the anxiety
options.B: Explain the procedure simply and check their understanding
options.C: Give a sedative medication
options.D: Call the doctor to cancel the test

explanation: Clear, simple explanations reduce anxiety and ensure the patient understands before diagnostic procedures begin. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T2#GNS311_U3_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary function of the cornea in the eye?

options.A: Bending incoming light rays
options.B: Changing shape for focus
options.C: Producing aqueous humor
options.D: Transmitting nerve impulses

explanation: The transparent cornea acts as the eye's outermost lens, providing most of the optical power to bend and focus light. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h1)

question: A patient loses the ability to see color in dim lighting. Which retinal structure is likely affected?

options.A: Rod cells
options.B: Cone cells
options.C: Optic nerve fibers
options.D: Corneal epithelium

explanation: Rod photoreceptors are specialized for vision in dim light, while cones handle detailed color vision in bright light. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h1)

question: Myopia is commonly known by which clinical term?

options.A: Presbyopia
options.B: Farsightedness
options.C: Nearsightedness
options.D: Astigmatism

explanation: Myopia causes light rays to focus in front of the retina, making close objects clear while distant objects look blurry. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h2)

question: Why does presbyopia typically develop in older adults?

options.A: The cornea becomes permanently opaque
options.B: Retinal receptor cells permanently die
options.C: The natural lens loses its flexibility
options.D: Intraocular pressure increases rapidly

explanation: Aging causes hardening of the crystalline lens, reducing accommodation for near vision tasks like reading. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h2)

question: What is the medical term for inflammation of the conjunctiva?

options.A: Keratitis
options.B: Uveitis
options.C: Conjunctivitis
options.D: Glaucoma

explanation: Conjunctivitis refers to inflammation of the clear membrane lining the eyelids and covering the sclera. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h3)

question: A patient presents with a red, painful eye and thick purulent discharge. What nursing intervention is priority?

options.A: Preparing the patient for immediate laser surgery
options.B: Massaging the tear ducts every two hours
options.C: Teaching proper hand hygiene and infection control
options.D: Applying a tight eye patch to reduce movement

explanation: Infectious conjunctivitis spreads easily, making strict handwashing and hygiene essential to prevent outbreaks. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary pathophysiology underlying most types of glaucoma?

options.A: Clouding of the natural crystalline lens
options.B: Increased intraocular pressure damaging the optic nerve
options.C: Degeneration of the central macula on the retina
options.D: Bacterial infection of the anterior chamber

explanation: Glaucoma damages optic nerve fibers due to pressure buildup from trapped fluid within the eye. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which symptom distinguishes acute angle-closure glaucoma from open-angle glaucoma?

options.A: Purulent discharge from the eyelid
options.B: Gradual loss of peripheral vision
options.C: Painless blurring of central vision
options.D: Severe eye pain and colored halos

explanation: Acute angle-closure causes a rapid pressure spike, triggering severe pain, headache, nausea, and halos around lights. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h4)

question: A cataract is characterized by which physical change in the eye?

options.A: Thinning of the outer cornea
options.B: Detachment of the sensory retina
options.C: Clouding of the crystalline lens
options.D: Elevation of intraocular pressure

explanation: Protein clumping inside the lens causes opacification, preventing clear light transmission to the retina. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h5)

question: Which area of vision is primarily affected by age-related macular degeneration?

options.A: Color vision
options.B: Night vision
options.C: Central vision
options.D: Peripheral vision

explanation: The macula handles high-acuity tasks like reading and facial recognition, which are impaired in AMD while peripheral vision remains intact. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h5)

question: What is the immediate nursing action for a patient with a chemical splash in the eye?

options.A: Flush the eye with continuous water or saline irrigation
options.B: Remove any visible foreign bodies with dry cotton swabs
options.C: Apply an antibiotic ointment and a tight pressure patch
options.D: Instill anesthetic drops to relieve sharp burning pain

explanation: Immediate, prolonged irrigation dilutes and removes chemical agents before they can cause severe corneal damage. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid removing an embedded object from a penetrating eye injury?

options.A: It might trigger severe allergic skin reactions
options.B: The object helps keep the eyelid open for drainage
options.C: Foreign objects dissolve naturally within a few hours
options.D: Removal can cause internal ocular contents to escape

explanation: Pulling out an embedded object removes the tamponade effect, potentially leading to prolapse of intraocular structures. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h6)

question: A patient who underwent cataract surgery asks if they can lift heavy grocery bags. What is the correct nursing response?

options.A: Heavy lifting is safe as long as you do not bend your knees
options.B: Avoid heavy lifting because it increases intraocular pressure
options.C: Wait until tomorrow morning before lifting heavy objects
options.D: Light lifting is permitted if you wear dark sunglasses

explanation: Heavy lifting, straining, and bending increase venous pressure and IOP, risking wound rupture and hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of wearing a rigid shield over the eye at night after surgery?

options.A: Absorbing any normal serous drainage from the wound
options.B: Preventing accidental rubbing or trauma during sleep
options.C: Filtering out bright ultraviolet light from overhead bulbs
options.D: Keeping prescribed medicated eye drops inside the socket

explanation: Sleeping poses a risk of unconsciously rubbing the healing eye against bedding, which can disrupt surgical incisions. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T3#GNS311_U3_T3_h7)

question: What part of the eye provides most of its optical focusing power?

options.A: The flexible lens
options.B: The pigmented iris
options.C: The clear cornea
options.D: The vascular retina

explanation: The cornea is the outermost transparent layer that bends incoming light rays to provide the primary refractive power of the eye. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h1)

question: The primary function of the rods and cones in the retina is to do what?

options.A: Adjust the size of the pupil
options.B: Produce clear aqueous humor fluid
options.C: Convert light into electrical impulses
options.D: Lubricate the outer corneal surface

explanation: Photoreceptors like rods and cones absorb light energy and translate it into neural signals that travel via the optic nerve to the brain. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which structure is responsible for the continuous production of aqueous humor?

options.A: The cornea endothelium
options.B: The ciliary body
options.C: The trabecular meshwork
options.D: The Schlemm canal

explanation: Specialized tissue in the ciliary body secretes aqueous humor into the posterior chamber of the eye. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h2)

question: A blockage within the trabecular meshwork will immediately lead to what physiological change?

options.A: Dilation of the retinal veins
options.B: Decreased aqueous production
options.C: Clouding of the crystalline lens
options.D: Increased intraocular pressure

explanation: When the main drainage channel is blocked while fluid continues to production occurs, aqueous humor accumulates and raises pressure inside the globe. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h2)

question: The primary structural damage in glaucoma occurs in which part of the eye?

options.A: The optic nerve head
options.B: The center of the lens
options.C: The pigmented iris layer
options.D: The surface of the cornea

explanation: Glaucoma damages retinal ganglion cell axons where they exit the eye at the optic nerve head, causing progressive vision loss. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h3)

question: Angle-closure glaucoma differs from open-angle glaucoma because angle-closure presents with which feature?

options.A: Normal resistance within the trabecular mesh
options.B: A slow, completely painless loss of vision
options.C: An abrupt, painful spike in pressure
options.D: Delayed swelling of the crystalline lens

explanation: Physical blockage of the drainage angle causes a sudden, highly painful elevation of intraocular pressure requiring immediate intervention. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is the primary pathological change that occurs inside a cataractous lens?

options.A: Inflammation of the ciliary muscle
options.B: Atrophy of the outer corneal layer
options.C: Excessive production of aqueous humor
options.D: Denaturation and clumping of proteins

explanation: Structural proteins in the lens break down and aggregate, scattering light and destroying lens transparency. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h4)

question: A patient with an early cataract most commonly complains about which visual symptom?

options.A: Severe itching and thick purulent discharge
options.B: Flashing lights followed by floating webs
options.C: Glare from bright lights and blurry vision
options.D: Sudden severe pain and complete blindness

explanation: Clumped proteins scatter incoming light rays, creating noticeable blurriness and troublesome glare, particularly during night driving. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary trigger for the growth of abnormal blood vessels in proliferative diabetic retinopathy?

options.A: Elevated intraocular pressure
options.B: Retinal tissue hypoxia
options.C: Bacterial corneal infection
options.D: Rapid protein clumping

explanation: Damaged capillaries fail to deliver adequate oxygen, creating localized hypoxia that stimulates the release of growth factors for new blood vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h5)

question: A client experiencing degeneration of the macular area will primarily notice loss of what visual function?

options.A: Color shade differentiation
options.B: Night time vision capacity
options.C: Outer peripheral boundaries
options.D: Sharp central vision

explanation: The macula contains the highest concentration of cones responsible for detailed central tasks like reading and facial recognition. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h5)

question: Uveitis refers to inflammation primarily affecting which layer of the eye?

options.A: The uveal tract
options.B: The clear cornea
options.C: The inner retina
options.D: The fibrous sclera

explanation: Uveitis is the inflammation of the middle vascular layer of the eye, which includes the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h6)

question: Why can severe intraocular inflammation lead to a secondary rise in pressure?

options.A: The cornea thickens and blocks light entry
options.B: The lens swells instantly from bacterial toxins
options.C: Retinal vessels constrict and stop fluid flow
options.D: Inflammatory cells clog the drainage meshwork

explanation: White blood cells and protein debris shed during inflammation can obstruct the trabecular meshwork, hindering aqueous humor outflow. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h6)

question: What do cotton-wool spots observed during a retinal examination typically represent?

options.A: Bacterial colonies growing on the retina
options.B: Accumulated clumps of lens protein
options.C: Deposits of unabsorbed aqueous humor
options.D: Localized areas of nerve fiber ischemia

explanation: Cotton-wool spots are fluffy white patches caused by microvascular occlusion and subsequent infarction of the nerve fiber layer. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical retinal finding in chronic systemic hypertension?

options.A: Flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages
options.B: Cotton-wool ischemic patches
options.C: Arteriolar narrowing and thickening
options.D: Purulent corneal ulcerations

explanation: Corneal ulcers stem from local trauma or infection, whereas hypertensive retinopathy affects retinal blood vessels and nerve layers. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h7)

question: What symptom reported by a patient is considered an urgent ophthalmic red flag?

options.A: Gradual blurring of distant text
options.B: Sudden severe eye pain with halos
options.C: Intermittent dry eye discomfort
options.D: Mild itching from seasonal allergies

explanation: Acute onset eye pain accompanied by halos around lights often signals angle-closure glaucoma, which is a medical emergency. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h8)

question: A patient recovering from intraocular surgery should be instructed to avoid which activity?

options.A: Straining heavily during bowel movements
options.B: Sleeping with the head slightly elevated
options.C: Eating soft foods without added salt
options.D: Walking slowly around the hospital room

explanation: Straining, heavy lifting, or bending over increases venous pressure and intraocular pressure, which can disrupt surgical incisions. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T4#GNS311_U3_T4_h8)

question: What is the primary function of the Eustachian tube?

options.A: Equalizing pressure in the middle ear
options.B: Amplifying sound waves in the inner ear
options.C: Producing cerumen to protect the ear canal
options.D: Filtering dust particles from nasal passages

explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx to maintain equal pressure on both sides of the tympanic membrane. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why are young children more prone to middle ear infections?

options.A: Their Eustachian tubes are shorter and more horizontal
options.B: Their mastoid air cells are fully developed at birth
options.C: Their tympanic membranes are thicker than adult membranes
options.D: They produce excessive cerumen in the external canal

explanation: A horizontal and shorter Eustachian tube allows pathogens from the nasopharynx to easily enter the middle ear space. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h1)

question: What does a normal, healthy tympanic membrane look like during an otoscopic exam?

options.A: Dark blue with fluid bubbles
options.B: Pearly gray and translucent
options.C: Bright red and bulging
options.D: Yellow and opaque

explanation: A normal tympanic membrane is typically pearly gray, translucent, and reflects a clear cone of light. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h2)

question: A patient is scheduled for a diagnostic test to measure middle ear compliance. Which test should the nurse expect?

options.A: Computed tomography scan
options.B: Fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy
options.C: Tympanometry
options.D: Pure-tone audiometry

explanation: Tympanometry measures how the tympanic membrane responds to changes in air pressure, indicating middle ear function. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h2)

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of otitis externa when manipulating the ear?

options.A: Complete loss of high-frequency hearing
options.B: Instant relief from severe pressure
options.C: Nausea accompanied by severe nystagmus
options.D: Intense pain when pulling the pinna

explanation: Inflammation of the external ear canal makes pulling or pressing on the pinna or tragus very painful. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h3)

question: What is a primary dietary modification for a patient diagnosed with Meniere's disease?

options.A: Restriction of fluid volume
options.B: High protein intake
options.C: Low sodium intake
options.D: Elimination of dairy products

explanation: Reducing dietary sodium helps decrease fluid retention and endolymphatic pressure within the inner ear. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h3)

question: Where do most anterior nosebleeds originate in the nasal cavity?

options.A: Kiesselbach's plexus
options.B: The superior turbinate
options.C: The olfactory bulb
options.D: The sphenoid sinus ostia

explanation: Kiesselbach's plexus is a vascular network located on the anterior nasal septum that is the most frequent site for nosebleeds. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h4)

question: What advice should a nurse give a patient using an over-the-counter nasal decongestant spray?

options.A: Use the spray continuously until all sinus pressure disappears
options.B: Limit use to three to five days to prevent rebound congestion
options.C: Tilt the head backward fully before releasing each dose
options.D: Dilute the medication with sterile water if stinging occurs

explanation: Overusing topical nasal decongestants leads to rhinitis medicamentosa, where congestion worsens significantly when the drug wears off. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why is using a tongue depressor contraindicated when a patient is suspected of having epiglottitis?

options.A: It introduces bacterial pathogens into the larynx
options.B: It can trigger sudden, complete airway obstruction
options.C: It causes severe bleeding from the tonsillar pillars
options.D: It distorts the visual field of the vocal cords

explanation: Manipulating an inflamed epiglottis with a tongue depressor can cause reflex laryngospasm and total airway closure. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which clinical manifestation is most characteristic of a peritonsillar abscess?

options.A: Painless swelling of the parotid gland
options.B: Trismus and a muffled voice
options.C: White patches on the tympanic membrane
options.D: Clear nasal discharge and sneezing

explanation: Peritonsillar abscess causes difficulty opening the mouth (trismus) and produces a characteristic thickened or muffled voice. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is often the earliest sign of bleeding in a patient who just had a tonsillectomy?

options.A: A sudden drop in systemic blood pressure
options.B: Frequent swallowing while at rest
options.C: Complaints of severe pain in the ears
options.D: Bright red emesis containing large clots

explanation: Patients who swallow repeatedly while resting or sleeping are likely swallowing trickling blood from the surgical site. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h6)

question: What essential equipment must be kept at the bedside immediately following a laryngectomy?

options.A: Nasal speculum and topical vasoconstrictors
options.B: Audiometric testing headphones
options.C: Emergency tracheostomy and suction kit
options.D: Tympanometry compliance probe

explanation: Immediate airway access via a tracheostomy kit and suction equipment is critical for managing sudden airway occlusion or secretion buildup. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why is a button battery lodged in the nasal cavity considered an urgent medical emergency?

options.A: It blocks the Eustachian tube and impairs hearing
options.B: It causes rapid tissue necrosis and chemical burns
options.C: It immediately expands upon contact with nasal mucus
options.D: It triggers an immediate systemic anaphylactic shock

explanation: Button batteries release electrical current and caustic leakage that quickly burn through mucosal tissue and cartilage. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h7)

question: What clinical sign indicates acute upper airway obstruction caused by laryngeal edema?

options.A: Stridor
options.B: Epistaxis
options.C: Otalgia
options.D: Tinnitus

explanation: Stridor is a high-pitched, turbulent airflow sound resulting from narrowing or obstruction of the upper airway. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T5#GNS311_U3_T5_h7)

question: Which tube links the middle ear to the back of the throat to balance pressure?

options.A: Eustachian tube
options.B: Ostiomeatal complex
options.C: Cochlear duct
options.D: Olfactory bulb

explanation: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, helping to equalize pressure and drain fluids. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h1)

question: What main process fails first in many common ear, nose, and throat infections?

options.A: Disruption of normal mucociliary clearance
options.B: Hyperactivity of the primary gustatory nerves
options.C: Excessive production of systemic antibodies
options.D: Rapid regeneration of squamous epithelial cells

explanation: When the tiny hairs and mucus layer stop clearing properly, fluid builds up and lets germs grow easily. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h1)

question: What causes a stuffy nose during a common cold?

options.A: Atrophy of the olfactory receptors
options.B: Rapid destruction of the acoustic nerve
options.C: Submucosal gland hypersecretion and edema
options.D: Calcification of the nasal cartilage

explanation: Inflammation makes blood vessels leak and glands pump out extra fluid, which swells up the nasal passages. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h2)

question: Why does a simple cold often turn into a bacterial sinus infection?

options.A: The immune system completely stops producing white blood cells
options.B: Cold air freezes the protective cilia inside the nasal passages
options.C: Viruses actively convert normal flora into pathogenic bacteria
options.D: Mucosal swelling blocks sinus drainage pathways and traps bacteria

explanation: Swelling closes off the tiny openings where sinuses drain, trapping fluid and bacteria inside. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h2)

question: What type of hearing loss does a buildup of earwax (cerumen) cause?

options.A: Conductive hearing loss
options.B: Sensorineural hearing loss
options.C: Functional hearing loss
options.D: Central processing loss

explanation: Earwax blocking the canal stops sound waves from traveling through to the eardrum, causing conductive hearing loss. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h3)

question: What happens inside the inner ear during Meniere's disease?

options.A: Abnormal accumulation of endolymph fluid
options.B: Severe atrophy of the external ear canal
options.C: Complete calcification of the ossicles
options.D: Rupture of the tympanic membrane

explanation: Meniere's disease happens when fluid builds up in the inner ear chambers, increasing pressure. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h3)

question: Which tiny loose particles in the inner ear cause positional vertigo (BPPV)?

options.A: Ossicles
options.B: Otoliths
options.C: Cerumen
options.D: Tympanic membrane

explanation: Loose calcium crystals, or otoliths, float into the inner ear canals and send false balance signals to the brain. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why does turning over in bed sometimes trigger a sudden spinning sensation?

options.A: Inappropriate stimulation of hair cells by floating crystals
options.B: Complete destruction of the auditory cortex in the brain
options.C: Sudden bacterial infection of the external auditory meatus
options.D: Accumulation of thick wax pressing against the eardrum

explanation: Head movement shifts loose crystals across sensitive hair cells, making the brain feel like the room is spinning. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h4)

question: Besides dead white blood cells and debris, what else makes up the pus seen on infected tonsils?

options.A: Epithelial bone
options.B: Bacteria
options.C: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.D: Dissolved cerumen

explanation: White blood cells cluster together with bacteria and dead tissue to form the white patches seen during tonsillitis. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why can a sinus infection in the cheek make your upper teeth ache?

options.A: Inflammation of the throat closes the main Eustachian tube opening
options.B: The roots of the upper teeth lie very close to the floor of the maxillary sinus
options.C: Increased intracranial pressure forces fluid down into the dental pulp
options.D: Infection spreads directly down the facial nerve into the mandible

explanation: The roots of top teeth sit right below the maxillary sinus, so sinus pressure easily feels like a toothache. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h5)

question: What are the soft, non-cancerous growths that form in the nose from long-term allergies?

options.A: Cholesteatomas
options.B: Otic capsules
options.C: Tonsillar stones
options.D: Nasal polyps

explanation: Ongoing irritation and swelling inside the nose can cause soft, teardrop-shaped growths called nasal polyps. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h6)

question: What causes the airway to close up during sleep in someone with obstructive sleep apnea?

options.A: Relaxation of upper airway dilator muscles
options.B: Excessive drying of the laryngeal mucosa
options.C: Sudden paralysis of the diaphragm muscle
options.D: Complete cessation of brainstem respiratory signals

explanation: When throat muscles relax deeply during sleep, the airway can easily collapse and block breathing. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is the most common type of cancer found in the throat and voice box?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma
options.B: Small cell sarcoma
options.C: Adenocarcinoma
options.D: Basal cell carcinoma

explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma starts in the flat, skin-like cells lining the inside of the throat and mouth. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why do cancers high up in the back of the nose often first show up as a lump in the neck?

options.A: The nasopharynx has a dense network of lymphatic vessels that drain to the neck
options.B: Viral infections cause generalized swelling of all regional sweat glands
options.C: The primary cancer site migrates downward into the thyroid gland
options.D: Tumors in this region rapidly invade the carotid artery and form cysts

explanation: The head and neck have many lymph channels, making it easy for cancer cells to travel to nearby lymph nodes. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h7)

question: Infection around the eye (orbital cellulitis) most commonly spreads from which nearby area?

options.A: Ethmoid or sphenoid sinuses
options.B: The external ear canal
options.C: The lateral vocal cords
options.D: The soft palate mucosa

explanation: Sinus infections can spread easily across the thin bone walls straight into the eye socket. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h8)

question: Why can a severe sinus infection cause swelling around the eye and trouble moving it?

options.A: Complete obstruction of the Eustachian tube altering intraocular pressure
options.B: Systemic allergic reaction causing generalized fluid retention in the face
options.C: Metastatic spread of abnormal lymphoid cells to the lacrimal gland
options.D: Direct extension of infection through the thin lamina papyracea into the orbit

explanation: The bone separating the ethmoid sinus from the eye is very thin, allowing bacteria to cross over and cause swelling. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T6#GNS311_U3_T6_h8)

question: How should a nurse pull the pinna when performing an otoscopic exam on an adult?

options.A: Upward and backward
options.B: Downward and backward
options.C: Straight outward
options.D: Downward and forward

explanation: Pulling the adult pinna upward and backward straightens the external auditory canal for a clear view of the tympanic membrane. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why is checking nasal patency a necessary part of a basic EENT assessment?

options.A: To check for fluid balance in the body
options.B: To confirm adequate airflow through each nostril
options.C: To measure the exact intracranial pressure
options.D: To test the function of the optic nerve

explanation: Assessing nasal patency ensures that the nasal passages are clear of major obstructions hindering normal breathing. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h1)

question: A patient with chronic open-angle glaucoma is most likely to experience which symptom?

options.A: Total blindness within twenty-four hours
options.B: Excessive tearing and thick discharge
options.C: Severe sudden eye pain and redness
options.D: Gradual loss of peripheral vision

explanation: Chronic open-angle glaucoma develops slowly and painlessly, typically causing a subtle loss of peripheral vision first. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h2)

question: Which activity should a patient strictly avoid immediately following cataract surgery?

options.A: Walking across the room
options.B: Speaking in a normal tone
options.C: Bending below the waist
options.D: Eating soft solid foods

explanation: Bending below the waist increases intraocular pressure, which can disrupt the delicate surgical site inside the eye. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h2)

question: Why must ear drop medications be warmed to room temperature before administration?

options.A: To prevent severe vertigo and dizziness
options.B: To kill harmful bacteria in the canal
options.C: To numb the tympanic membrane
options.D: To dissolve hard earwax instantly

explanation: Cold ear drops stimulate the inner ear vestibular system, triggering sudden and severe dizziness or vertigo. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h3)

question: When is ear canal irrigation strictly contraindicated for managing cerumen impaction?

options.A: When the earwax is dark brown in color
options.B: When a tympanic membrane perforation is suspected
options.C: When the client is an older adult
options.D: When the patient complains of mild itching

explanation: Irrigating an ear with a perforated eardrum allows fluid to enter the middle ear space, potentially introducing infection. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h3)

question: A patient with a nosebleed should sit upright and lean forward primarily to...

options.A: prevent blood from entering the pharynx
options.B: reduce the need for direct pressure
options.C: make nasal packing easier to insert
options.D: increase the blood pressure in the head

explanation: Leaning forward keeps blood from pooling in the throat, protecting the patient from swallowing blood or aspirating. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h4)

question: What is a key indicator of continuous bleeding after nasal surgery?

options.A: Frequent swallowing by the patient
options.B: Dry lips and mild thirst
options.C: A slightly elevated body temperature
options.D: Clear nasal discharge

explanation: Frequent swallowing strongly suggests that blood is trickling down the back of the throat from the surgical site. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h4)

question: What is the best initial position for a patient recovering from a tonsillectomy who is still drowsy?

options.A: High Fowler upright position
options.B: Flat on the back supine
options.C: Trendelenburg position
options.D: Side-lying or semi-prone

explanation: A side-lying position allows oral secretions and blood to drain safely out of the mouth rather than pooling in the airway. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why are red or brown colored liquids avoided immediately after a tonsillectomy?

options.A: They can be mistaken for fresh or old blood
options.B: They cause severe allergic reactions in children
options.C: They delay the return of the normal gag reflex
options.D: They irritate the delicate throat incision directly

explanation: Avoiding red or dark liquids ensures that if the patient vomits, true blood is not confused with ingested beverage coloring. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why should a nurse apply gentle pressure to the nasolacrimal duct after instilling eye drops?

options.A: To reduce pain and pressure inside the eyeball
options.B: To keep the eyelid tightly closed during sleep
options.C: To help spread the drop evenly across the cornea
options.D: To prevent systemic absorption of the medication

explanation: Nasolacrimal occlusion blocks the drug from entering the nasal mucosa and passing into the bloodstream where it could cause side effects. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h6)

question: Which of the following practices is dangerous when administering nasal sprays?

options.A: Keeping the container upright during administration
options.B: Blowing the nose gently before applying the medication
options.C: Directing the spray tip straight toward the nasal septum
options.D: Closing the opposite nostril during the actuation
