explanation: Directing the spray toward the septum can damage the delicate mucosal tissue and trigger nosebleeds. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h6)

question: A home safety assessment for a patient with severe visual impairment should prioritize...

options.A: removing loose rugs and clear pathways
options.B: installing bright flashing strobe lights
options.C: arranging all furniture against walls
options.D: purchasing a specialized talking clock

explanation: Clearing physical obstacles and loose rugs directly prevents dangerous falls for patients with low vision. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary message a nurse should emphasize to a newly diagnosed glaucoma patient?

options.A: Surgical intervention replaces the need for medications
options.B: Vision loss from glaucoma can always be reversed later
options.C: Prescribed eye drops must be used every day for life
options.D: Eye pressure only rises when experiencing severe headaches

explanation: Glaucoma is a chronic condition requiring lifelong daily medication adherence to control intraocular pressure and protect vision. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T7#GNS311_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of rehabilitation in special senses disorders?

options.A: Preventing the initial onset of sensory diseases
options.B: Completely reversing permanent sensory loss
options.C: Maximizing residual function and adapting to deficits
options.D: Restoring normal anatomical structure of the organ

explanation: Rehabilitation focuses on helping patients adapt to permanent changes and make the best use of their remaining senses since complete reversal is often impossible. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why does vestibular dysfunction pose a severe safety hazard to patients?

options.A: It causes complete and irreversible hearing loss
options.B: It impairs the ability to read small printed text
options.C: It leads to a total loss of facial muscle control
options.D: It drastically increases the risk of dangerous falls

explanation: Vestibular disorders disrupt balance and spatial orientation, which directly leads to instability and frequent falls. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which tool is commonly used by nurses to evaluate visual acuity?

options.A: Ophthalmoscope
options.B: Tympanic probe
options.C: Audiometer
options.D: Snellen chart

explanation: The Snellen chart is the standard clinical tool used to measure visual acuity at a specific distance. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h2)

question: What should a comprehensive nursing assessment for sensory deficits always include besides physical testing?

options.A: Screening for home environmental safety hazards
options.B: Performing complex surgical evaluations
options.C: Prescribing appropriate assistive optical lenses
options.D: Administering intravenous antibiotic therapies

explanation: Evaluating the living environment is critical to protect visually or aurally impaired patients from preventable accidents and injuries. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of orientation and mobility training for a blind patient?

options.A: Restoring full color vision to damaged photoreceptors
options.B: Strengthening the muscles surrounding the eyeball
options.C: Safe and independent movement through the environment
options.D: Improving reading speed using high-contrast texts

explanation: Orientation and mobility training teaches individuals how to navigate their surroundings safely using tools like white canes. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h3)

question: How do non-optical aids assist patients living with low vision?

options.A: By surgically replacing the clouded crystalline eye lens
options.B: By directly stimulating the optic nerve with electrical currents
options.C: By correcting refractive errors through laser corneal surgery
options.D: By using environmental modifications like large prints and tactile markers

explanation: Non-optical aids rely on environmental adjustments, tactile cues, and enlarged items to enhance daily functioning without prescription lenses. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h3)

question: What is the function of a cochlear implant in severe hearing loss?

options.A: Vibrating the bones of the skull to conduct sound waves
options.B: Removing obstructive cerumen from the tympanic membrane
options.C: Amplifying ambient sounds through the external ear canal
options.D: Directly stimulating the auditory nerve, bypassing damaged hair cells

explanation: Cochlear implants use electronic devices to bypass damaged inner ear structures and stimulate the auditory nerve directly. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why is shouting discouraged when speaking to a person with a hearing impairment?

options.A: It causes immediate sensorineural fatigue in the listener
options.B: It distorts the spoken words and makes comprehension harder
options.C: It damages the delicate cochlear implants they are wearing
options.D: It violates professional communication standards in the ward

explanation: Raising the pitch and volume into a shout distorts speech sounds, making it more difficult for a hearing-impaired person to understand. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the goal of canalith repositioning maneuvers in vestibular disorders?

options.A: Draining excess endolymph fluid from the cochlear duct
options.B: Strengthening the extraocular muscles of the eye
options.C: Shifting misplaced otoconia out of the semicircular canals
options.D: Relieving pressure behind the tympanic membrane

explanation: Canalith repositioning maneuvers move loose calcium debris out of sensitive inner ear canals to stop vertigo spells. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h5)

question: How do gaze stabilization exercises help patients with vestibular dysfunction?

options.A: They increase the production of inner ear fluid
options.B: They train the brain to integrate visual and balance signals
options.C: They improve the physical strength of the neck vertebrae
options.D: They prevent the buildup of cerumen in the ear canal

explanation: Gaze stabilization helps the brain compensate for lost inner ear function by coordinating eye movements with head motion. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h5)

question: A patient with sudden vision loss refuses to leave home and appears withdrawn. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Limit family visits to prevent them from becoming overly dependent
options.B: Insist that they immediately return to their normal work routine
options.C: Tell them that blindness is easy to manage with modern technology
options.D: Acknowledge their emotional distress and explore peer support groups

explanation: Validating feelings and connecting patients with peers helps combat the isolation and depression common in sensory loss. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is a primary benefit of vocational rehabilitation for individuals with sensory impairments?

options.A: Modifying workplaces to help them maintain employment
options.B: Dispensing specialized hearing aids free of charge
options.C: Training family members to perform household chores
options.D: Providing medical cures for degenerative eye diseases

explanation: Vocational rehabilitation focuses on job retention and workplace modifications to ensure continued economic independence. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T8#GNS311_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is a primary reason sensory deficits often go unnoticed in community settings?

options.A: Patients always report symptoms immediately
options.B: Sensory organs regenerate quickly on their own
options.C: Limited access to routine specialized care
options.D: Special senses do not affect daily functioning

explanation: Many individuals lack regular screening opportunities, allowing conditions to progress silently. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h1)

question: How do nurses primarily contribute to public health regarding sensory disorders?

options.A: Prescribing specialized antibiotic eye drops
options.B: Manufacturing affordable hearing aids locally
options.C: Performing complex surgical lens replacements
options.D: Identifying early functional losses at the frontline

explanation: Community nurses act as the first point of contact for detecting early signs of sensory decline. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h1)

question: Which deficiency does Vitamin A supplementation specifically help prevent in young children?

options.A: Xerophthalmia
options.B: Cataracts
options.C: Glaucoma
options.D: Presbyopia

explanation: Vitamin A is vital for corneal health, and its deficiency leads to dryness and potential blindness known as xerophthalmia. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is the direct link between measles vaccination and eye health?

options.A: It cures congenital cataracts during infancy
options.B: It reduces intraocular pressure in glaucoma patients
options.C: It prevents corneal scarring caused by measles infections
options.D: It stops the normal aging process of the lens

explanation: Severe measles infections can cause corneal ulcers and scarring, which immunization successfully averts. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is the primary tool used to measure distant visual acuity in literate adults?

options.A: Snellen chart
options.B: Tonometer
options.C: Ophthalmoscope
options.D: Otoscope

explanation: The Snellen chart features standardized rows of letters used to evaluate how well a person sees from a distance. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h3)

question: A nurse wants to perform a quick, non-invasive bedside evaluation of a patient's hearing. Which method is most appropriate?

options.A: Caloric testing
options.B: Tympanometry
options.C: Whisper test
options.D: Audiometry booth

explanation: The whisper test is a simple, quick screening tool that requires no special equipment at the bedside. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h3)

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention in sensory disorders?

options.A: Limit disability and maximize remaining function
options.B: Prevent the initial onset of the disease
options.C: Cure the underlying genetic pathology completely
options.D: Eliminate all environmental noise pollution

explanation: Tertiary prevention focuses on rehabilitation and helping individuals adapt to established, irreversible deficits. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h4)

question: Which intervention represents tertiary care for a patient with permanent vision loss?

options.A: Administering prophylactic eye drops at birth
options.B: Vaccinating the community against measles
options.C: Training in the use of a white cane
options.D: Screening school children with the Snellen chart

explanation: Mobility training with assistive devices helps individuals manage existing permanent visual impairment. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why is adequate home lighting particularly critical for patients with visual impairments?

options.A: It reverses the pathological progression of cataracts
options.B: It stimulates the regeneration of retinal photoreceptor cells
options.C: It maximizes remaining vision and prevents accidental falls
options.D: It completely cures age-related macular degeneration

explanation: Good illumination helps individuals with low vision navigate safely and utilize whatever visual capacity they have left. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h5)

question: Which nursing counseling point is essential regarding the use of unprescribed eye drops?

options.A: Avoid them because they can cause severe tissue damage
options.B: Store them in direct sunlight to maintain potency
options.C: Use them freely as long as they are herbal preparations
options.D: Share leftover drops with family members experiencing symptoms

explanation: Unprescribed or traditional concoctions often introduce harmful contaminants or chemicals, risking permanent eye injury. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse within a multidisciplinary sensory care team?

options.A: Coordinating care and linking the patient with specialists
options.B: Manufacturing customized hearing aid devices
options.C: Replacing the role of the audiologist entirely
options.D: Performing independent ophthalmic surgeries

explanation: Nurses centralize communication and ensure smooth referrals between patients and various specialized therapists. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h6)

question: Which specialist is primarily consulted when a patient requires a detailed evaluation of hearing loss?

options.A: Physiotherapist
options.B: Ophthalmologist
options.C: Dietitian
options.D: Audiologist

explanation: Audiologists specialize in evaluating, diagnosing, and managing hearing and balance disorders. [learn more](GNS311_U3_T9#GNS311_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the main goal of aseptic technique in clinical practice?

options.A: To completely destroy every single spore on surgical steel
options.B: To eliminate the need for routine handwashing in wards
options.C: To clean visibly dirty floors in the emergency unit
options.D: To prevent the transfer of pathogens to vulnerable sites

explanation: Aseptic technique creates a barrier that keeps harmful microorganisms away from susceptible areas of the body. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h1)

question: How does aseptic technique differ from complete sterilization?

options.A: Aseptic technique minimizes microbes while sterilization eliminates all forms
options.B: Aseptic technique relies solely on chemical sprays without barriers
options.C: Sterilization is only used for nurse uniforms and patient beds
options.D: Sterilization is performed exclusively by patients at home

explanation: Sterilization destroys all microbial life including spores, whereas asepsis reduces microbe counts to safe levels. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which procedure requires strict surgical asepsis rather than medical asepsis?

options.A: Administering routine oral paracetamol tablets
options.B: Assisting a patient to eat a meal
options.C: Checking blood pressure with a manual cuff
options.D: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter

explanation: Urinary catheterization enters a sterile body cavity, demanding surgical asepsis to prevent infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h2)

question: A nurse gives a bed bath to an adult patient. Which practice is being applied?

options.A: Terminal disinfection
options.B: Absolute sterilization
options.C: Surgical asepsis
options.D: Medical asepsis

explanation: Routine daily nursing care uses clean technique to reduce pathogen transmission without needing a completely sterile environment. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h2)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infection spread in a hospital?

options.A: Proper hand hygiene
options.B: Wearing heavy boots
options.C: Opening ward windows
options.D: Changing bed sheets daily

explanation: Cleaning hands removes transient microorganisms acquired from patient contact and environment surfaces. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h3)

question: When is handwashing with soap and water preferred over alcohol hand rub?

options.A: When leaving a clean administrative office
options.B: Before touching a patient on intact skin
options.C: Immediately after taking a patient's pulse
options.D: When hands are visibly dirty or soiled

explanation: Soap and physical friction are required to remove organic material and visible dirt that alcohol rubs cannot wash away. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h3)

question: Which item of PPE is removed first when doffing after a procedure?

options.A: Gown
options.B: Gloves
options.C: Mask
options.D: Goggles

explanation: Gloves carry the highest microbial load after patient contact and are removed first to prevent contaminating other items. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why must a nurse still clean their hands immediately after taking off medical gloves?

options.A: Gloves make the skin too dry without extra water rinsing
options.B: Microbes can pass through microscopic tears or pinholes in gloves
options.C: Soap activates the latex material to make it safer for skin
options.D: Hospital policy requires double washing for aesthetic reasons

explanation: Gloves are not entirely impermeable, making hand hygiene mandatory after doffing to eliminate unseen contamination. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h4)

question: What part of a sterile drape or field is considered unsterile?

options.A: The absolute exact center
options.B: The top surface facing upwards
options.C: The area touched by sterile forceps
options.D: The outer one-inch border

explanation: The edge of the sterile wrapper touches unsterile surfaces during setup, making the outer margin non-sterile. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h5)

question: A nurse accidentally drops a sterile forceps onto the nursing station floor. What action should be taken?

options.A: Wipe it quickly with spirit and place it back on the tray
options.B: Keep using it if the floor looks visibly clean and dry
options.C: Wash it with ward soap and use it for the procedure
options.D: Discard the forceps and obtain a new sterile replacement

explanation: Contact with the floor immediately compromises sterility, requiring a replacement tool to prevent infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h5)

question: Which finding is a local sign of infection at a wound site?

options.A: Clear urine output
options.B: Normal resting pulse
options.C: Purulent discharge
options.D: Stable blood pressure

explanation: Pus or purulent drainage indicates white blood cells fighting local bacterial invasion at the wound site. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h6)

question: How does proper aseptic technique lower the rate of hospital-acquired infections?

options.A: By eliminating the need for nurses to monitor vital signs
options.B: By reducing the financial cost of purchasing intravenous fluids
options.C: By shortening the number of days patients spend in the outpatient clinic
options.D: By stopping exogenous and endogenous pathogens from entering vulnerable tissues

explanation: Blocking microbial entry during invasive clinical tasks prevents germs from establishing colonies inside the patient. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T1#GNS311_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of closing a skin laceration with sutures?

options.A: To prevent the need for tetanus shots
options.B: To eliminate all local blood supply
options.C: To completely eliminate scar tissue
options.D: To promote primary intention healing

explanation: Bringing clean wound edges together speeds up primary intention healing and reduces scarring. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is the time elapsed since the injury important when deciding to suture?

options.A: Suture threads dissolve faster in older wounds
options.B: Skin loses all its natural elasticity overnight
options.C: Bacterial multiplication increases significantly after twelve hours
options.D: Local anesthesia stops working after six hours have passed

explanation: Wounds older than twelve hours carry a much higher risk of trapping bacteria inside if closed immediately. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h1)

question: What check must always happen distal to a limb laceration before suturing?

options.A: Bone density scan
options.B: Blood glucose level
options.C: Neurovascular status
options.D: Body mass index

explanation: Checking movement, feeling, and blood flow below the injury ensures nerves and vessels are intact. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h2)

question: When is a tetanus booster usually indicated for a laceration injury?

options.A: If the patient has never experienced a fever before
options.B: Every time any patient receives a single skin stitch
options.C: When the last dose was over five to ten years ago
options.D: Only when the wound was caused by a clean kitchen knife

explanation: Outdated tetanus immunity leaves the patient vulnerable to infection, making vaccination status vital during assessment. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h2)

question: Where should you NEVER use a local anesthetic containing epinephrine?

options.A: Large thigh muscles
options.B: Fingers and toes
options.C: The upper back area
options.D: The chest wall skin

explanation: Epinephrine constricts blood vessels so severely in end-artery digits that it can cause tissue death. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is the main benefit of adding epinephrine to a local anesthetic solution?

options.A: It makes the suture needle slide through skin much faster
options.B: It completely sterilizes the local wound area
options.C: It reduces bleeding and extends anesthesia duration
options.D: It eliminates the need for any physical cleaning

explanation: Vasoconstriction keeps the drug local longer and gives a clearer, bloodless field to work in. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is the most effective method for reducing bacteria inside an open wound?

options.A: High-pressure saline irrigation
options.B: Scrubbing with dry gauze pads
options.C: Applying antibiotic ointment first
options.D: Soaking in warm soapy water

explanation: Physical flushing with sterile saline washes away loose bacteria and microscopic particles effectively. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why should harsh chemical antiseptics be kept out of an open wound bed?

options.A: They change the color of the patient's skin permanently
options.B: They damage healthy tissue and delay healing
options.C: They cause the suture thread to break down instantly
options.D: They immediately dissolve the local anesthetic drug

explanation: Toxic chemicals harm host cells just as much as bacteria, impairing the natural repair process. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h4)

question: Which suture material is typically used for closing the outer skin layer?

options.A: Vicryl
options.B: Catgut
options.C: Monocryl
options.D: Nylon

explanation: Nylon is a strong non-absorbable material ideal for outer skin where it will later be removed. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h5)

question: Where on the suture needle should the needle holder be clamped?

options.A: At the very end of the trailing thread
options.B: One-third to halfway from the swaged end
options.C: Directly in the exact middle of the curve
options.D: Right at the sharp tip of the needle

explanation: Clamping at this point provides stability and prevents the needle from bending during tissue entry. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h5)

question: At what angle should the suture needle enter the skin surface?

options.A: 90 degrees
options.B: 15 degrees
options.C: 45 degrees
options.D: 180 degrees

explanation: Entering perpendicular to the skin surface allows the curved needle to rotate smoothly through the tissue. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the main advantage of using simple interrupted sutures?

options.A: If one stitch fails or gets infected, the others remain intact
options.B: They eliminate the need for any local numbing agents
options.C: They take half the time to complete compared to staples
options.D: They never leave any marks or scarring on the skin

explanation: Because every single knot is tied separately, a single failure does not compromise the whole wound. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h6)

question: What substance is often recommended to keep a fresh suture line moist?

options.A: Petroleum jelly
options.B: Povidone-iodine scrub
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide
options.D: Alcohol wipe solution

explanation: Keeping a wound moist with petroleum jelly prevents heavy scab formation and helps minimize scarring. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h7)

question: Why should patients avoid soaking a freshly sutured wound in water?

options.A: It softens the tissue and increases infection risk
options.B: Water instantly dissolves the non-absorbable nylon
options.C: Soaking causes the skin edges to fuse together too fast
options.D: Moisture prevents the local anesthesia from wearing off

explanation: Prolonged water immersion can introduce bacteria and macerate delicate healing skin edges. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h7)

question: Which body area generally requires the shortest time before suture removal?

options.A: The face
options.B: The shin area
options.C: The knee joint
options.D: The lower back

explanation: Facial skin heals rapidly due to excellent blood supply, and early removal prevents permanent track marks. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h8)

question: Why should you pull the cut suture thread toward the wound line during removal?

options.A: To keep the scissors from getting dull too quickly
options.B: To prevent pulling surface bacteria through the tissue tract
options.C: To ensure the patient feels less pulling sensation
options.D: To make the knot easier to grab with sterile forceps

explanation: Pulling away from the wound can pop the healing edges back open or drag contaminated surface thread through the deeper skin. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h8)

question: What is the most common adverse outcome following simple laceration repair?

options.A: Wound infection
options.B: Severe allergic shock
options.C: Bone infection
options.D: Nerve paralysis

explanation: Bacteria introduced during injury or procedural steps can multiply, making infection the leading complication. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h9)

question: Which of the following is NOT a classic sign of a localized wound infection?

options.A: Cool skin temperature
options.B: Localized swelling
options.C: Expanding redness
options.D: Purulent discharge

explanation: Infection typically causes increased blood flow and inflammation, which feels warm or hot to the touch rather than cool. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T2#GNS311_U4_T2_h9)

question: What is the primary clinical goal of emergency wound management?

options.A: Covering the defect with tight bandages
options.B: Applying strong topical antibiotics immediately
options.C: Stopping bleeding with chemical cautery
options.D: Restoring tissue integrity and preventing infection

explanation: Emergency wound care focuses primarily on closing the defect properly while keeping bacteria out to ensure optimal healing. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why does the time since an injury happen matter when treating a wound?

options.A: Wounds older than twelve hours have a much higher infection risk
options.B: Sutures dissolve faster if placed too late
options.C: Local anesthetics stop working effectively after six hours
options.D: Skin elasticity decreases rapidly within the first hour

explanation: Bacteria multiply significantly over time in open tissue, making delayed primary closure safer for older wounds. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which local anesthetic agent is most commonly used for emergency wound suturing?

options.A: Lignocaine
options.B: Ketamine
options.C: Atropine
options.D: Diazepam

explanation: Lignocaine provides rapid and reliable local nerve blockade for minor surgical procedures in the emergency setting. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h2)

question: Where should you avoid injecting local anesthetic mixed with adrenaline?

options.A: The anterior thigh
options.B: The scalp region
options.C: Fingers and toes
options.D: The abdominal wall

explanation: Adrenaline causes vasoconstriction which can cut off blood supply entirely in end-arterial digits, leading to tissue death. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the main reason for cleaning out and removing tissue from a wound before closing it?

options.A: Enlarging the incision for better visibility
options.B: Diluting bacterial load with sterile water
options.C: Stimulating immediate collagen synthesis
options.D: Removing dead and contaminated tissue

explanation: Debridement clears away non-viable tissue that would otherwise support bacterial growth and delay proper healing. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why is gentle washing preferred over high-pressure spraying for dirty wounds?

options.A: It activates the local anesthetic solution more effectively
options.B: It ensures the sterile saline warms up to body temperature
options.C: It reduces the total volume of fluid required for the procedure
options.D: It prevents driving bacteria deeper into the underlying tissue

explanation: Excessive pressure during irrigation can force surface contaminants further into microscopic tissue planes, worsening the infection risk. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which type of thread is non-absorbable and usually chosen for closing skin cuts?

options.A: Nylon
options.B: Monocryl
options.C: Vicryl
options.D: Catgut

explanation: Nylon is a non-absorbable synthetic polymer that elicits minimal tissue reaction and is standard for skin surface closure. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why do nurses and doctors use a cutting needle when stitching up a skin cut?

options.A: It prevents the suture thread from fraying under tension
options.B: It dissolves safely inside the subcutaneous fat layer
options.C: It easily penetrates tough, fibrous dermal tissue
options.D: It eliminates the need for administering local anesthesia

explanation: Skin is a tough, fibrous organ; a cutting needle has a built-in blade edge that smoothly slices a path through it. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the main benefit of using simple interrupted stitches?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for subcutaneous stitches
options.B: If one stitch fails, the remaining sutures keep the wound secure
options.C: It is the fastest method to close very long lacerations
options.D: It requires fewer instruments than any other closure method

explanation: Because each stitch is tied separately, a localized complication or failure will not compromise the entire wound closure. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which stitching method works best to make sure the skin edges roll slightly outward?

options.A: Subcutaneous buried stitch
options.B: Vertical mattress suture
options.C: Simple running suture
options.D: Simple interrupted suture

explanation: The vertical mattress technique incorporates deep and superficial bites that naturally flip the skin edges outward, preventing depressed scars. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: About how many days after stitching should facial skin sutures be removed?

options.A: 21 to 28 days
options.B: Immediate removal
options.C: 10 to 14 days
options.D: 5 to 7 days

explanation: Facial skin heals rapidly and has a rich blood supply, so sutures are removed early to prevent permanent cross-hatch marks. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h6)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of an early surgical site infection?

options.A: Clear serous fluid draining within the first hour
options.B: Spreading erythema and warmth around the wound edges
options.C: Temporary numbness directly beneath the repaired skin
options.D: Mild itching sensation during the third week of healing

explanation: Progressive redness, heat, and throbbing pain indicate bacterial proliferation requiring prompt clinical re-evaluation. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary content inside a superficial abscess cavity?

options.A: Clear serous fluid only
options.B: Pure arterial blood supply
options.C: Pus and necrotic tissue
options.D: Fresh granulation tissue cells

explanation: An abscess is formed by the accumulation of pus, which consists of white blood cells, bacteria, and dead tissue. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why does a superficial abscess present with localized warmth and redness?

options.A: Blocked lymphatic drainage from the muscle
options.B: Superficial nerve fiber irritation alone
options.C: Increased blood flow to the infected area
options.D: Decreased cellular metabolism in the skin

explanation: Inflammation causes vasodilation, bringing more blood to the site to fight infection, which creates heat and redness. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which microorganism is most frequently responsible for superficial skin abscesses?

options.A: Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Klebsiella pneumoniae
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Staphylococcus aureus remains the leading pathogen cultured from cutaneous abscesses worldwide. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h2)

question: How do bacteria typically gain entry to cause a soft tissue abscess?

options.A: Through a break in the skin barrier
options.B: Via direct diffusion across intact epidermis
options.C: Through systemic arterial embolism events
options.D: Via retrograde lymphatic flow from the bone

explanation: Pathogens require a compromised skin barrier, such as a scrape, puncture, or hair follicle micro-tear, to enter subcutaneous tissue. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h2)

question: What physical finding indicates that an abscess is ready for incision and drainage?

options.A: Absent skin color
options.B: Complete anesthesia
options.C: Hard induration
options.D: Fluctuation

explanation: Fluctuation confirms the presence of liquid pus within a walled-off cavity, indicating it is ready to be drained. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h3)

question: A patient with a hand abscess has a high fever and a fast heart rate. What does this suggest?

options.A: Systemic spread of the infection
options.B: Normal local inflammatory response
options.C: Immediate resolution of the abscess
options.D: Successful containment by white cells

explanation: Systemic signs like fever and tachycardia mean the infection is affecting the whole body, requiring urgent clinical attention. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which location represents a major contraindication for routine bedside incision and drainage?

options.A: The upper region of the shoulder
options.B: The lateral aspect of the thigh
options.C: The posterior surface of the forearm
options.D: The central face and nasal triangle

explanation: Facial infections near the nose carry risks of intracranial extension via venous sinuses, requiring specialist management. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h4)

question: Why is a bleeding disorder considered a relative contraindication for minor surgical drainage?

options.A: It prevents the formation of any pus cavity
options.B: It increases the risk of prolonged local hemorrhage
options.C: It accelerates bacterial growth within the wound
options.D: It stops local anesthetics from working properly

explanation: Patients with clotting abnormalities may bleed excessively from the incision site, requiring closer hemostatic control. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of using hemostats inside an opened abscess cavity?

options.A: To irrigate the deep tissue with cold saline
options.B: To break up internal loculations and pockets of pus
options.C: To suture the skin edges tightly closed immediately
options.D: To measure the exact pH level of the exudate

explanation: Hemostats are gently opened inside the cavity to disrupt walled-off chambers and ensure complete drainage of all pus. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h5)

question: Why must sterile technique be maintained during an incision and drainage procedure?

options.A: To prevent the scalpel blade from becoming dull too quickly
options.B: To prevent introducing new bacteria into the open wound
options.C: To ensure the local anesthetic numbs the skin faster
options.D: To keep the surrounding skin completely dry at all times

explanation: A sterile field stops external contaminants from entering the surgical site and causing secondary infections. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h5)

question: Why is local anesthetic injected around the abscess perimeter rather than directly into it?

options.A: Peripheral injection numbs the deeper bone faster
options.B: Direct injection is less effective due to acidic pH in pus
options.C: Direct injection causes the pus to spread into blood vessels
options.D: It prevents the abscess cavity from bursting prematurely

explanation: Infected tissue is acidic, which neutralizes local anesthetics and makes direct injection painful and ineffective. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h6)

question: The primary purpose of placing gauze packing inside a drained abscess cavity is to...

options.A: keep the wound edges open for continued drainage
options.B: stimulate rapid skin scar tissue formation
options.C: deliver high doses of systemic oral antibiotics
options.D: absorb all local arterial blood supply permanently

explanation: Packing prevents the superficial skin from sealing over before the deeper cavity heals from the inside out. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h6)

question: How soon is the first follow-up visit typically scheduled after an incision and drainage?

options.A: After one month
options.B: 1 to 2 weeks
options.C: 3 to 4 weeks
options.D: 24 to 48 hours

explanation: An early follow-up within two days is essential to check for complications and remove or adjust packing material. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h7)

question: What is the preferred method for an incision and drainage wound to heal?

options.A: Primary intention
options.B: Immediate closure
options.C: Secondary intention
options.D: Tertiary intention

explanation: Abscess cavities are left open to heal by secondary intention from the base upward to prevent trapping bacteria. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h7)

question: Why are antibiotics unnecessary for many simple, small superficial abscesses?

options.A: Surgical drainage removes the infected source completely
options.B: The body clears all remaining bacteria instantly without help
options.C: Bacteria inside an abscess never respond to drugs
options.D: Antibiotics cannot reach soft tissues under any circumstance

explanation: Once the pus and bacteria are physically evacuated, the body's immune system often clears the remaining localized infection without drugs. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h8)

question: When should a clinician definitely prescribe systemic antibiotics following an abscess drainage?

options.A: Only when the patient requests pain medication
options.B: If the incision was made using a small scalpel
options.C: For every single routine subcutaneous skin boil
options.D: If the patient has severe surrounding cellulitis

explanation: Extensive surrounding tissue inflammation or systemic symptoms require adjunctive systemic antibiotic therapy. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h8)

question: What warning sign should prompt a patient to return immediately after an abscess drainage?

options.A: Fever and spreading redness around the wound
options.B: Mild itching around the adhesive bandage
options.C: Gradual fading of the initial bruise color
options.D: Slight clear fluid on the gauze dressing

explanation: Expanding erythema and fever indicate worsening infection or spreading cellulitis that requires prompt medical review. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h9)

question: Which complication is most commonly associated with squeezing a facial skin boil?

options.A: Permanent transformation into bone tissue
options.B: Instantaneous healing without any scarring
options.C: Spreading infection into intracranial venous sinuses
options.D: Complete immunity from future skin boils

explanation: Squeezing facial boils can force bacteria backward through valveless veins into the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T4#GNS311_U4_T4_h9)

question: What anatomical structure is removed during male circumcision?

options.A: The foreskin
options.B: The scrotal sac
options.C: The frenulum
options.D: The glans penis

explanation: Circumcision specifically targets the prepuce, which is the loose fold of skin covering the head of the penis. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is male circumcision often done for medical reasons besides religion?

options.A: To stop testosterone production
options.B: To cure all sexually transmitted infections
options.C: To increase penile length
options.D: For better hygiene and disease prevention

explanation: Removing the foreskin reduces the buildup of smegma and lowers the risk of certain infections. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h1)

question: What is the medical term for a foreskin that cannot be pulled back over the head of the penis?

options.A: Hypospadias
options.B: Phimosis
options.C: Balanitis
options.D: Paraphimosis

explanation: Phimosis describes a tight prepuce that cannot be retracted over the glans penis. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h2)

question: A newborn has hypospadias. What should be done regarding circumcision?

options.A: Perform it immediately to stop infections
options.B: Apply high-dose antibiotics first
options.C: Defer the procedure to save tissue for surgical repair
options.D: Use a Plastibell device instead of a blade

explanation: Urological conditions like hypospadias mean the foreskin is needed later by surgeons to repair the misplaced urinary opening. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which family health history is most critical to check before a baby's circumcision?

options.A: Hypertension
options.B: Bleeding disorders
options.C: Diabetes mellitus
options.D: Asthma attacks

explanation: Conditions like hemophilia create severe bleeding risks during surgery, making a bleeding history check mandatory. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h3)

question: You notice severe diaper rash on an infant's genitals just before a scheduled circumcision. What is the best action?

options.A: Give oral antibiotics and start immediately
options.B: Apply petroleum jelly and cut anyway
options.C: Proceed quickly before the rash worsens
options.D: Postpone the procedure until the skin heals

explanation: Broken skin or active infection in the surgical area greatly increases the risk of wound contamination. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h3)

question: How does a Plastibell device remove extra foreskin?

options.A: By dissolving the tissue with chemical paste
options.B: By burning the skin away with an electric current
options.C: By cutting off blood supply until the tissue falls off
options.D: By crushing the tissue flat before cutting

explanation: A tied suture stops blood flow to the foreskin over the plastic ring, causing the tissue to die and drop off naturally. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which instrument uses a metal bell and plate to crush the foreskin before cutting?

options.A: Mogen clamp
options.B: Plastibell device
options.C: Surgical laser
options.D: Gomco clamp

explanation: The Gomco clamp uses a bell-and-plate design to crush blood vessels and tissue before the surgeon snips away the excess skin. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h4)

question: What local anesthetic additive must be avoided when injecting the penis?

options.A: Sterile water
options.B: Epinephrine
options.C: Normal saline
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate

explanation: Epinephrine causes strong blood vessel constriction, which can cut off blood flow to the penis and lead to tissue death. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why is a dorsal penile nerve block given before a newborn circumcision?

options.A: To block pain signals from the surgical site
options.B: To cause tissue swelling that stops bleeding
options.C: To speed up wound healing
options.D: To relax the leg muscles

explanation: Local nerve blocks stop pain pathways, helping to manage pain during genital surgery. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h5)

question: What substance is usually applied to a fresh circumcision dressing to stop it from sticking?

options.A: Petroleum jelly
options.B: Povidone-iodine gel
options.C: Methylated spirit
options.D: Hydrogen peroxide

explanation: Petroleum ointment creates a barrier that prevents healing tissue from sticking to diapers or clothing. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why is checking and documenting the first urination after a circumcision important?

options.A: To confirm the urethra is open and working normally
options.B: To calculate total urine output for the shift
options.C: To check if kidneys filter excess drugs
options.D: To prove the baby is fully hydrated

explanation: Checking the first void ensures that swelling or surgery has not caused urinary retention. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the most common immediate complication after male circumcision?

options.A: Urethral stricture
options.B: Erectile failure
options.C: Scrotal swelling
options.D: Hemorrhage

explanation: Bleeding from the surgical cut is a frequent acute complication that needs direct pressure or stitches. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h7)

question: What complication happens if a Plastibell device slips down onto the penile shaft days after the procedure?

options.A: Kidneys stop filtering urine
options.B: Permanent loss of bladder control
options.C: Tissue strangulation and lack of blood flow
options.D: Foreskin grows back instantly

explanation: A slipped ring acts like a tourniquet, cutting off blood supply and risking tissue death if not removed quickly. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h7)

question: A mother is worried about a yellow coating on her baby's healing circumcision site. How should you explain this?

options.A: Anesthetic is leaking out
options.B: It is a normal part of healing
options.C: It is a severe bacterial infection
options.D: Diaper ointment was applied incorrectly

explanation: A yellowish layer commonly forms over a healing genital wound and is not pus or infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is an important instruction for parents whose infant has a Plastibell device in place?

options.A: Soak the infant in strong salt water to dissolve it
options.B: Pull the plastic ring gently every morning
options.C: Apply hot compresses to melt the plastic away
options.D: Allow the ring to fall off on its own without pulling it

explanation: Pulling or forcing the Plastibell ring off too early can cause heavy bleeding and incomplete skin separation. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T5#GNS311_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of administering medication via the intravenous route?

options.A: Slower and sustained drug release
options.B: Elimination of all potential adverse reactions
options.C: Bypassing the need for sterile equipment
options.D: Immediate bioavailability in the bloodstream

explanation: Injecting fluids directly into a vein bypasses absorption barriers, delivering the substance immediately to systemic circulation. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: A patient requires rapid fluid resuscitation for severe dehydration. Why is the intravenous route selected over the oral route?

options.A: It avoids the cost of purchasing oral medications
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from filtering the fluids
options.C: It stimulates the digestive tract to absorb water
options.D: It restores circulating blood volume much faster

explanation: Intravenous infusion provides rapid volume expansion, which is critical in emergency dehydration and shock scenarios. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h1)

question: Where should a nurse begin when selecting a peripheral vein for cannulation?

options.A: The most proximal sites near the shoulder joint
options.B: The large veins in the upper arm or shoulder
options.C: The internal jugular vein in the neck
options.D: The most distal sites on the upper extremities

explanation: Starting distally preserves higher venous sites on the same limb if complications arise and a new line is needed. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Why is the antecubital fossa typically avoided for routine, long-term peripheral infusions?

options.A: Medications given there take too long to reach the heart
options.B: Arm bending can easily occlude or dislodge the cannula
options.C: Skin infections are completely unavoidable in elbow creases
options.D: The veins in this area have too many valves to pass a needle

explanation: Movement at the elbow joint creates mechanical stress that frequently kinks the catheter or irritates the vessel wall. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which intravenous fluid category expands the intravascular volume without causing major fluid shifts into cells?

options.A: Hypotonic solutions
options.B: Colloidal suspensions
options.C: Isotonic solutions
options.D: Hypertonic solutions

explanation: Isotonic fluids share a similar osmolarity with blood plasma, keeping water balanced inside the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: A patient with cerebral edema requires a fluid that will draw excess water out of swollen brain cells. What type of fluid is indicated?

options.A: Pure sterile water
options.B: Hypertonic solution
options.C: Hypotonic solution
options.D: Isotonic solution

explanation: Hypertonic solutions create a higher concentration gradient in the blood, pulling fluid out of tissues and cells. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying a tourniquet prior to peripheral IV cannulation?

options.A: To engorge and make the superficial veins visible
options.B: To numb the skin area before needle insertion
options.C: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the limb
options.D: To sterilize the puncture site against bacteria

explanation: A tourniquet traps venous blood in the limb, filling the veins and making them easier to palpate and puncture. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: Which IV cannula gauge is most appropriate for a patient receiving rapid blood transfusion?

options.A: 24 gauge
options.B: 26 gauge
options.C: 22 gauge
options.D: 18 gauge

explanation: Larger bore needles with a smaller gauge number, like 18G, prevent hemolysis and allow viscous blood to flow rapidly. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h4)

question: At what angle should a nurse typically insert a peripheral IV cannula into the skin?

options.A: 5 to 10 degrees flat
options.B: 15 to 30 degrees
options.C: 90 degrees straight down
options.D: 45 to 60 degrees

explanation: A 15 to 30-degree angle allows the needle to pierce the skin and enter the superficial vein without puncturing through the back wall. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is it necessary to let the skin antiseptic air dry completely before inserting the IV catheter?

options.A: To allow the chemical time to destroy microorganisms
options.B: To stop the vein from collapsing during needle entry
options.C: To prevent the antiseptic from stinging the patient's skin
options.D: To ensure the transparent dressing sticks to the area

explanation: Antiseptics like alcohol and chlorhexidine require adequate contact and drying time to achieve their maximal antimicrobial effect. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h5)

question: What does a micro-drip infusion set typically deliver per milliliter of fluid?

options.A: 20 drops
options.B: 10 drops
options.C: 15 drops
options.D: 60 drops

explanation: Micro-drip sets always deliver 60 drops per milliliter, making them ideal for precise volume control in pediatrics. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: A nurse calculates an IV drop rate incorrectly, causing fluid to infuse far too quickly. What immediate risk does this pose?

options.A: Rapid crystallization of electrolytes in blood
options.B: Immediate collapse of all peripheral veins
options.C: Permanent numbness of the infused limb
options.D: Circulatory overload and pulmonary edema

explanation: Infusing fluids too rapidly overwhelms the cardiovascular system, leading to elevated blood pressure and fluid in the lungs. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h6)

question: How often should a nurse routinely inspect a peripheral intravenous infusion site?

options.A: Whenever the intravenous fluid bag runs completely empty
options.B: During every nursing shift or per hospital policy
options.C: Only when the patient complains of sharp pain
options.D: Once every twenty-four hours during bed bath

explanation: Routine checks ensure early detection of localized complications like infiltration, phlebitis, or accidental dislodgement. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Why do nurses flush intermittent peripheral IV catheters with normal saline?

options.A: To cool down the internal lining of the vein
options.B: To stimulate local blood flow back to the heart
options.C: To dilute any medication previously given too fast
options.D: To clear residual blood and keep the lumen open

explanation: Saline flushes clear blood from the catheter tip, preventing clots from forming and occluding the cannula. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which sign is most characteristic of intravenous fluid infiltration into surrounding tissues?

options.A: Swelling and coolness around the insertion site
options.B: Severe itching across the entire chest wall
options.C: Bleeding around the transparent dressing tape
options.D: Hard red streaks tracking up the upper arm

explanation: When room-temperature IV fluid enters subcutaneous tissue instead of the vein, the area becomes swollen and cool to the touch. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: What is the priority nursing action when a nurse suspects phlebitis at a peripheral IV site?

options.A: Flush the line firmly with saline to clear the vessel
options.B: Administer a prescribed oral pain reliever for comfort
options.C: Stop the infusion and remove the cannula immediately
options.D: Slow down the infusion rate and apply an ice pack

explanation: Removing the catheter halts further irritation to the vein wall and prevents worsening inflammation or infection. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h8)

question: What action should a nurse take immediately after withdrawing a peripheral IV cannula?

options.A: Apply a cold ice pack directly over the bare wound
options.B: Massage the puncture site vigorously to stimulate flow
options.C: Instruct the patient to bend the elbow joint tightly
options.D: Apply firm, continuous pressure to the site with gauze

explanation: Direct pressure prevents hematoma formation and stops bleeding from the puncture wound in the vein. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: Why is it important to pull the cannula out parallel to the skin surface during removal?

options.A: To prevent trauma and scraping of the internal vein wall
options.B: To ensure the plastic catheter tip does not break off
options.C: To allow the skin to close up faster without a bandage
options.D: To make sure the tape comes off without pulling hair

explanation: Withdrawing the cannula at the same low angle it entered prevents the tip from scraping or tearing the vessel lumen. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T6#GNS311_U4_T6_h9)

question: What is the primary focus of cancer epidemiology in healthcare?

options.A: Tracking disease frequency and distribution in populations
options.B: Discovering single-gene mutations in laboratory mice
options.C: Treating individual patients in hospital surgical wards
options.D: Manufacturing chemotherapy drugs for clinical trials

explanation: Epidemiology looks at populations rather than single patients to understand disease patterns. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do health ministries rely on epidemiological data for public health?

options.A: To determine individual nursing shift rosters and pay
options.B: To calculate daily hospital food budgets for patients
options.C: To allocate medical resources and plan health infrastructure
options.D: To diagnose rare tropical infections in emergency rooms

explanation: Population data guides the distribution of healthcare resources where they are needed most. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which cancer types are among the most commonly diagnosed in Nigeria?

options.A: Testicular and thyroid cancers
options.B: Brain tumors and bone sarcomas
options.C: Skin melanoma and acute leukemia
options.D: Breast, cervical, and prostate cancers

explanation: Breast, cervical, and prostate cancers form the bulk of the cancer burden in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a primary reason for poor cancer survival outcomes in Nigeria?

options.A: Universal free healthcare covering all treatments
options.B: Late presentation of patients at health facilities
options.C: Excessive availability of advanced screening machines
options.D: Rapid genetic mutation rates unique to the region

explanation: Most patients arrive at advanced stages due to delays in seeking care and financial barriers. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What term describes the number of new cancer cases diagnosed in a population over a specific time?

options.A: Morbidity
options.B: Incidence
options.C: Mortality
options.D: Prevalence

explanation: Incidence specifically counts newly diagnosed cases during a defined period. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: How does prevalence differ from incidence in epidemiological data?

options.A: Prevalence counts total existing cases, while incidence counts new cases
options.B: Prevalence only measures deaths, while incidence measures recoveries
options.C: Prevalence applies to animals, while incidence applies to humans
options.D: Prevalence is calculated weekly, while incidence is calculated yearly

explanation: Prevalence includes all current cases, whereas incidence tracks only newly diagnosed ones. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is an example of a modifiable cancer risk factor?

options.A: Advancing age
options.B: Biological sex
options.C: Family genetics
options.D: Tobacco smoking

explanation: Smoking is a behavior that an individual can alter, making it a modifiable risk factor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why is advancing age classified as a non-modifiable risk factor for cancer?

options.A: Age only affects infectious diseases rather than chronic ones
options.B: Medical science can easily reverse cellular aging processes
options.C: A person cannot alter the natural progression of getting older
options.D: Older adults never develop malignant tumors in clinical practice

explanation: Non-modifiable factors like age and genetics cannot be changed by personal choice or intervention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: What type of mutations account for the majority of cancer cases in human populations?

options.A: Inherited gene mutations from parents
options.B: Prenatal chromosomal abnormalities at birth
options.C: Somatic mutations acquired over a lifetime
options.D: Spontaneous mutations occurring only in red blood cells

explanation: Most cancers develop from acquired somatic mutations rather than inherited genetic traits. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: How do environmental carcinogens typically initiate the development of malignant tumors?

options.A: By stimulating excessive calcium absorption in the bones
options.B: By increasing the total volume of red blood cells in circulation
options.C: By lowering the resting heart rate of the affected patient
options.D: By damaging cellular DNA and overwhelming repair mechanisms

explanation: Carcinogens alter DNA, which can lead to uncontrolled cell growth if repairs fail. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of cancer screening programs in public health?

options.A: Administering high-dose chemotherapy to patients with advanced tumors
options.B: Conducting post-mortem autopsies to determine exact causes of death
options.C: Providing palliative comfort care for terminally ill hospital patients
options.D: Detecting pre-cancerous lesions or early-stage disease in asymptomatic people

explanation: Screening targets healthy individuals to catch diseases early before symptoms develop. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: Why is visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) useful for cervical cancer screening in resource-limited settings?

options.A: It can cure the cancer without needing any surgical intervention
options.B: It requires expensive machines and specialized pathology laboratories
options.C: It is a practical and low-cost alternative to complex laboratory tests
options.D: It replaces the need for any healthcare personnel during the procedure

explanation: VIA provides an affordable screening option where advanced equipment is unavailable. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is a key responsibility of nurses in cancer epidemiology and prevention?

options.A: Educating communities and contributing to cancer registries
options.B: Manufacturing pharmaceutical drugs in industrial laboratories
options.C: Funding public health research grants for universities
options.D: Performing major surgical resections of malignant tumors

explanation: Nurses educate the public and help record accurate data for cancer registries. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why is accurate nursing documentation essential for cancer registries?

options.A: It guarantees that patients will never experience side effects
options.B: It automatically lowers the cost of hospital admissions for patients
options.C: It replaces the need for doctors to diagnose malignant diseases
options.D: It provides researchers with reliable data to track disease trends

explanation: Precise records allow epidemiologists to monitor cancer patterns and evaluate interventions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of surgery when treating an early-stage solid tumor?

options.A: To destroy rapidly dividing systemic cells
options.B: To deliver targeted molecular therapy
options.C: To remove the primary tumor mass
options.D: To stimulate the patient immune system

explanation: Surgery involves physically cutting out the localized tumor tissue to control or cure the cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why is chemotherapy considered a systemic treatment?

options.A: It circulates through the entire bloodstream to reach cancer cells
options.B: It only affects cells located directly inside the targeted organ
options.C: It stimulates local antibodies without entering the vascular system
options.D: It relies entirely on high-energy radiation beams from outside

explanation: Chemotherapy drugs travel through the bloodstream, allowing them to reach cancer cells anywhere in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which major complication should a nurse watch out for after a major cancer surgery?

options.A: Venous thromboembolism
options.B: Permanent systemic hair loss
options.C: Immunotherapy toxicity
options.D: Acute radiation dermatitis

explanation: Having cancer and undergoing major surgery both raise the risk of blood clots forming in the deep veins. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the best way to prevent lung complications after major abdominal surgery?

options.A: Restrict fluid intake to prevent baseline edema
options.B: Administer scheduled intravenous chemotherapy agents
options.C: Apply specialized ionizing radiation shielding dressings
options.D: Encourage deep breathing and early ambulation

explanation: Deep breathing opens up the air sacs in the lungs while moving around gets the blood flowing, which stops the lungs from collapsing and prevents blood clots. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h2)

question: What must a nurse always check before giving chemotherapy through a peripheral line?

options.A: Total daily fluid intake limits
options.B: Blood return from the cannula
options.C: The patient room temperature
options.D: The exact family medical history

explanation: Seeing blood return confirms that the needle is securely inside the vein, preventing the drug from leaking into the surrounding tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why must nurses wear protective gear when handling chemotherapy drugs?

options.A: To stop airborne bacterial transmission from the patient
options.B: To protect the nurse from catching the patient malignancy
options.C: To prevent occupational exposure to hazardous cytotoxic agents
options.D: To keep the sterile intravenous tubing completely free of dust

explanation: Chemotherapy medications are strong drugs that can touch the skin or be breathed in, so staff need barriers to stay safe. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h3)

question: How should a nurse instruct a patient to care for skin undergoing radiation therapy?

options.A: Scrub the skin firmly with a rough sponge during baths
options.B: Apply strongly scented perfumed lotions twice a day
options.C: Expose the treatment field directly to strong sunlight daily
options.D: Wash the treatment area gently with mild soap and water

explanation: Gentle washing helps protect sensitive skin that has been weakened by radiation treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why does radiation therapy often cause skin breakdown?

options.A: Chemotherapy pills accumulate specifically in the subcutaneous fat layers
options.B: Ionizing radiation damages rapidly dividing basal cells in the epidermis
options.C: Surgical incisions fail to heal due to poor systemic hydration
options.D: Infection spreads rapidly from intravenous lines to the skin surface

explanation: Radiation affects normal, fast-growing skin cells along with the cancer cells, making it hard for the skin to heal and renew itself. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is a low count of white blood cells caused by cancer treatment called?

options.A: Erythrocytosis
options.B: Thrombocytopenia
options.C: Neutropenia
options.D: Hypercalcemia

explanation: Neutropenia is the medical term for a low number of neutrophils, which are white blood cells that fight off infections. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the best way to help a patient with painful mouth sores from chemotherapy?

options.A: Encourage the patient to consume very hot, spicy local meals
options.B: Provide frequent mouth rinses with a gentle, non-alcoholic solution
options.C: Scrub the oral lesions firmly with a stiff nylon toothbrush
options.D: Restrict all fluid intake to keep the oral cavity completely dry

explanation: Gentle rinses clean the mouth and soothe sores without causing more irritation to delicate tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h5)

question: What should you do first if a patient with neutropenia develops a fever?

options.A: Send the patient home to rest in a quiet environment
options.B: Wait for laboratory blood culture results for three days
options.C: Administer prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly
options.D: Apply cold ice packs to reduce systemic body temperature

explanation: Fever in a neutropenic patient is a medical emergency that needs immediate antibiotics to prevent severe infection. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: What causes tumor lysis syndrome to happen?

options.A: Rapid destruction of cancer cells releasing intracellular ions into blood
options.B: Sudden uncontrolled bleeding caused by severe bone marrow platelet failure
options.C: Infection spreading from the gastrointestinal tract into the bloodstream
options.D: Severe compression of the superior vena cava by a growing chest tumor

explanation: When cancer cells break down rapidly, they release cell contents into the blood faster than the kidneys can filter them out. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h6)

question: Why is cancer-related weight loss (cachexia) hard to fix just by eating more food?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs destroy the stomach lining permanently forever
options.B: Vitamins and minerals cannot be absorbed through human intestines
options.C: It involves complex metabolic and inflammatory alterations in the body
options.D: Patients simply refuse to eat because they dislike hospital food

explanation: Cachexia changes how the body handles proteins and energy due to inflammation, rather than just happening because the person is eating less. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: Which meal plan works best for a cancer patient who gets full quickly and has a poor appetite?

options.A: Serving small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals throughout the day
options.B: Restricting fluid intake completely during all daily waking hours
options.C: Forcing three large heavy meals regardless of patient comfort
options.D: Providing only clear water and plain broth for all nutrition

explanation: Eating small amounts often prevents the patient from feeling too full and helps them take in enough calories. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h7)

question: When is the best time to introduce palliative care for a patient with a serious cancer diagnosis?

options.A: After all medical and surgical treatment options fail completely
options.B: Only during the final twenty-four hours of active dying
options.C: Early in the disease trajectory alongside curative treatment
options.D: When the patient requests discontinuation of all nursing care

explanation: Palliative care improves comfort and quality of life, and it works best when started early while the patient is still receiving active treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the main goal of adding palliative care to cancer treatment?

options.A: Accelerating the terminal disease process to reduce hospital costs
options.B: Preventing family members from visiting the patient in the ward
options.C: Improving quality of life by managing pain and emotional distress
options.D: Replacing all standard chemotherapy protocols with herbal medicine

explanation: Palliative care focuses on whole-person comfort, helping manage physical symptoms and emotional stress for both the patient and their family. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T10#GNS321_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the main goal of cancer rehabilitation in modern care?

options.A: Prevent the initial development of primary malignancies
options.B: Replace traditional chemotherapy and radiation regimens
options.C: Maximize independence and enhance quality of life
options.D: Accelerate the rate of malignant cell proliferation

explanation: Cancer rehabilitation focuses on restoring physical and psychological functioning to improve the patient's daily life after treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why has cancer care shifted to include comprehensive rehabilitation?

options.A: Treatments frequently cause long-term physical and functional complications
options.B: Patients refuse traditional medical interventions entirely
options.C: Hospital stays need to be extended for financial reasons
options.D: Rehabilitation completely cures all types of advanced malignancies

explanation: Modern cancer therapies save lives but often leave patients with lasting side effects that require dedicated rehabilitative support. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which type of rehabilitation focuses on minimizing expected physical problems before they happen?

options.A: Preventive
options.B: Supportive
options.C: Palliative
options.D: Restorative

explanation: Preventive rehabilitation starts early to prepare the patient's body and reduce the severity of expected treatment side effects. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: A patient with advanced terminal cancer receives care focused only on comfort and pain relief. Which rehabilitation type is this?

options.A: Palliative
options.B: Preventive
options.C: Diagnostic
options.D: Restorative

explanation: Palliative rehabilitation prioritizes comfort, symptom management, and dignity for patients with advanced, life-limiting disease. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: Which professional helps patients adapt their daily activities and use assistive tools?

options.A: Occupational therapist
options.B: Physical therapist
options.C: Registered dietitian
options.D: Oncology social worker

explanation: Occupational therapists focus on enabling patients to perform everyday tasks safely using adaptive strategies and tools. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why is a team of different specialists essential for cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Physicians are unable to communicate directly with patients
options.B: Rehabilitation is too expensive for a single department to manage
options.C: Cancer affects multiple body systems requiring diverse specialized interventions
options.D: Hospital regulations mandate a minimum of five staff members per bed

explanation: The widespread physical and emotional impact of cancer demands varied expertise that only a collaborative team can provide. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is the purpose of tools like the Karnofsky Performance Scale?

options.A: Calculate the precise financial cost of hospital stays
options.B: Diagnose the exact histological subtype of a tumor
options.C: Determine the patient's exact genetic predisposition
options.D: Quantify functional decline and track recovery progress

explanation: Standardized scales provide objective measurements of a patient's functional ability and independence over time. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: A patient scheduled for physical therapy suddenly reports severe new bone pain and leg weakness. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Withhold therapy and notify the physician immediately for evaluation
options.B: Proceed with high-intensity resistance training to build muscle strength
options.C: Encourage the patient to walk off the pain using a supportive walker
options.D: Administer a mild sedative and document the findings at the end of the shift

explanation: New severe pain and weakness can indicate dangerous complications like spinal cord compression, requiring urgent medical review. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: How does cancer-related fatigue differ from normal tiredness?

options.A: It disappears immediately after completing a single nap
options.B: It is not relieved by standard periods of rest or sleep
options.C: It is caused strictly by lack of physical activity
options.D: It only occurs during the final stages of terminal illness

explanation: Cancer-related fatigue is a persistent, overwhelming exhaustion that does not resolve with normal rest or sleep patterns. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: A patient with severe fatigue struggles with morning baths and meals. What nursing action is best?

options.A: Teach energy conservation principles like prioritizing and pacing daily activities
options.B: Insist that the patient complete all chores at once to build endurance
options.C: Administer high-dose intravenous stimulants before every single meal
options.D: Discontinue all physical movement to preserve remaining body energy

explanation: Energy conservation helps patients manage limited stamina by spreading essential tasks throughout the day. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is a main benefit of regular exercise during cancer treatment?

options.A: Guarantees complete elimination of residual cancer cells
options.B: Prevents muscle atrophy and cardiovascular deconditioning
options.C: Reverses genetic mutations responsible for tumor growth
options.D: Eliminates the need for dietary nutritional supplements

explanation: Physical activity counters the debilitating deconditioning effects caused by prolonged bed rest and cytotoxic therapies. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Exercise plans for patients with bone cancer spread must include which safety step?

options.A: Maximum intensity weightlifting to strengthen weak bones
options.B: Modified weight-bearing activities to prevent pathological fractures
options.C: Complete avoidance of all upper body movement
options.D: High-impact running to stimulate bone density growth

explanation: Metastases weaken bone structure, requiring careful exercise modifications to protect the skeletal system from fractures. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why is untreated malnutrition dangerous for patients undergoing cancer therapy?

options.A: It immediately cures secondary opportunistic bacterial infections
options.B: It impairs wound healing and reduces overall treatment tolerance
options.C: It increases the physical growth rate of healthy muscle tissue
options.D: It prevents patients from feeling any psychological stress

explanation: Nutritional deficits compromise the body's ability to tolerate aggressive therapies and recover from surgical interventions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: A patient on chemotherapy has severe nausea and eats very little. What is the best nursing strategy?

options.A: Withhold all food until chemotherapy cycles are completely finished
options.B: Offer small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals throughout the day
options.C: Rely solely on intravenous fluids without any nutritional support
options.D: Force the patient to finish three large meals daily without exception

explanation: Small, frequent meals are easier for nauseated patients to tolerate compared to large, overwhelming food portions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: Which emotional response is common in individuals diagnosed with cancer?

options.A: Enhanced aggressive behavior toward healthcare staff
options.B: Complete emotional detachment and permanent euphoria
options.C: Anxiety, depression, and fear of disease recurrence
options.D: Sudden loss of all cognitive memory functions

explanation: The uncertainty and burden of cancer frequently cause significant anxiety, depressive symptoms, and fear of relapse. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: Why is addressing emotional distress important during cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Emotional well-being influences physical recovery and treatment adherence
options.B: Psychological counseling replaces the need for physical therapy
options.C: Mental health issues have no impact on overall survival rates
options.D: Patients prefer ignoring physical symptoms if they feel happy

explanation: Unmanaged emotional distress can hinder a patient's willingness and ability to participate in necessary rehabilitative therapies. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: What two core items are typically included in a survivorship care plan?

options.A: A prescription for lifetime chemotherapy and bed rest
options.B: A list of banned foods and prohibited physical exercises
options.C: A legal will and a detailed funeral arrangement binder
options.D: A treatment summary and a personalized follow-up schedule
