explanation: Survivorship plans summarize past treatments and outline recommended screenings and monitoring schedules for future health. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h9)

question: What is the main purpose of promoting healthy lifestyle habits in long-term cancer survivors?

options.A: Ensure the patient never visits a hospital department again
options.B: Replace the need for routine cancer surveillance screenings
options.C: Reduce recurrence risk and promote overall long-term wellness
options.D: Accelerate the natural aging process of body tissues

explanation: Healthy lifestyle choices help lower the risk of cancer recurrence and manage late side effects of past therapies. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h9)

question: What is the main feature of neoplastic diseases?

options.A: Uncontrolled and abnormal cell division
options.B: Sudden loss of normal blood circulation
options.C: Rapid healing of damaged body tissues
options.D: Permanent shrinkage of major internal organs

explanation: Neoplasms involve abnormal cells multiplying without the body's normal regulatory controls. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why do community health nurses place a strong focus on cancer prevention?

options.A: Neoplastic diseases are strictly contagious through casual physical contact
options.B: Treatment options are always completely free in government hospitals
options.C: Early detection completely eliminates the need for any follow-up care
options.D: Prevention significantly reduces overall disease burden and death rates

explanation: Stopping cancer early or preventing it altogether saves lives and lessens the impact on healthcare systems. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which prevention level includes routine screening tests like Pap smears?

options.A: Primary prevention
options.B: Secondary prevention
options.C: Tertiary prevention
options.D: Quaternary prevention

explanation: Screening aims to detect disease early before symptoms appear, which defines secondary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: A nurse teaches a client how to do regular breast self-examinations. Which prevention tier does this belong to?

options.A: Primordial prevention
options.B: Secondary prevention
options.C: Tertiary prevention
options.D: Primary prevention

explanation: Self-examinations and screenings catch health issues early, making them part of secondary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h2)

question: Administering the hepatitis B vaccine to infants is an example of which type of prevention?

options.A: Primary prevention
options.B: Secondary prevention
options.C: Diagnostic intervention
options.D: Tertiary prevention

explanation: Vaccines stop infections that can lead to cancer later in life, acting before disease starts. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: What is the main goal of primary cancer prevention counseling?

options.A: Managing side effects after chemotherapy
options.B: Minimizing exposure to environmental and lifestyle risk factors
options.C: Detecting small tumors before they cause pain
options.D: Providing comfort measures for terminal cancer patients

explanation: Primary prevention stops the disease process by reducing exposure to things that cause cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h3)

question: What is the main goal of secondary cancer prevention programs?

options.A: Preventing healthy individuals from encountering carcinogens
options.B: Providing emotional support to families
options.C: Detecting cancer early when treatment is most effective
options.D: Curing late-stage disease using advanced surgery

explanation: Early detection finds tumors at an early, manageable stage to improve survival outcomes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: A client asks why a screening test is recommended when they feel fine. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Doctors require everyone to complete these tests annually
options.B: Screenings find abnormal changes before symptoms or pain begin
options.C: It proves your immune system is completely free of infection
options.D: Healthy people have a higher risk of developing sudden tumors

explanation: Screening tests identify early cellular changes before clinical symptoms appear. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: When does tertiary prevention typically begin in a client's care timeline?

options.A: After a confirmed diagnosis and initial treatment
options.B: Prior to administering routine childhood immunizations
options.C: Before exposure to known environmental carcinogens
options.D: During routine community health screening outreaches

explanation: Tertiary prevention focuses on rehabilitation and managing complications after a disease has been diagnosed. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: A nurse teaches arm exercises to a client recovering from a mastectomy to prevent lymphedema. What type of prevention is this?

options.A: Primary prevention
options.B: Health promotion
options.C: Secondary prevention
options.D: Tertiary prevention

explanation: Managing post-treatment complications and supporting rehabilitation falls under tertiary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h5)

question: Why is genetic counseling recommended for individuals with a strong family history of cancer?

options.A: To replace the need for routine physical examinations
options.B: To cure existing genetic anomalies through diet
options.C: To guarantee the patient will never develop a tumor
options.D: To identify inherited risks and guide personal screening plans

explanation: Genetic counseling helps high-risk individuals understand their inherited risks and plan appropriate health monitoring. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which nursing action best supports effective patient education regarding cancer prevention?

options.A: Discouraging clients from asking questions
options.B: Handing out lengthy research journals without talking
options.C: Using complex medical jargon and Latin terms
options.D: Using simple language suited to the client's understanding

explanation: Clear communication ensures clients actually understand risk factors and follow preventive advice. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h6)

question: How does community-level nursing advocacy help reduce the rates of neoplastic diseases?

options.A: By manufacturing affordable chemotherapy drugs locally
options.B: By pushing for public policies that restrict exposure to carcinogens
options.C: By performing complex surgical tumor removals in rural clinics
options.D: By diagnosing hereditary gene mutations without labs

explanation: Advocacy involves changing laws and environments to protect entire communities from cancer-causing agents. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which activity is a direct example of a nurse engaging in community advocacy for cancer prevention?

options.A: Prescribing targeted drug therapies in a clinic
options.B: Participating in public campaigns to promote smoke-free public spaces
options.C: Performing routine microscope tissue checks in a lab
options.D: Discharging a client following uncomplicated surgery

explanation: Advocacy involves public health promotion and policy changes that protect populations from health risks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h7)

question: What triggers an oncologic emergency in a patient with cancer?

options.A: Sudden cessation of routine pain medication
options.B: Chronic malnutrition and long-term bed rest
options.C: Tumor growth or cancer treatment side effects
options.D: Bacterial infections acquired in the community

explanation: These crises arise directly from tumor expansion, spreading, or toxic effects of treatments like chemotherapy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why must nurses in general wards understand oncologic emergencies?

options.A: General ward nurses independently perform emergency surgeries
options.B: Nurses are required to administer specialized chemotherapy drugs
options.C: Patients can present with acute crises anywhere in the hospital
options.D: Oncologists rarely visit patients outside specialized cancer centers

explanation: Because cancer patients seek care in various hospital units, any nurse must recognize sudden life-threatening complications early. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h1)

question: Tumor lysis syndrome typically develops immediately after which event?

options.A: Surgical removal of a primary tumor
options.B: Prolonged periods of physical inactivity
options.C: Development of a secondary skin infection
options.D: Initiation of cytotoxic chemotherapy

explanation: The rapid destruction of cancer cells by chemotherapy releases large amounts of intracellular contents into the blood. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: What electrolyte imbalance is a hallmark feature of tumor lysis syndrome?

options.A: Hypercalcemia from bone breakdown
options.B: Hyponatremia from fluid overload
options.C: Hyperkalemia from cell destruction
options.D: Hypokalemia from excessive renal loss

explanation: Intracellular potassium floods the extracellular space when massive numbers of cancer cells break open simultaneously. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h2)

question: A patient with superior vena cava syndrome will most likely exhibit which physical sign?

options.A: Asymmetrical pupil dilation and nystagmus
options.B: Severe abdominal rigidity and rebound tenderness
options.C: Facial edema and neck vein distension
options.D: Lower extremity pitting edema and ulcers

explanation: Blocked blood return through the superior vena cava causes fluid to back up in the upper body and face. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: A cancer patient complains of new back pain and lower limb weakness. What is the priority nursing action?

options.A: Report symptoms immediately for possible spinal cord compression
options.B: Apply a warm compress to the lower back for muscle spasm
options.C: Administer oral laxatives to relieve suspected constipation
options.D: Encourage early ambulation to prevent deep vein thrombosis

explanation: New back pain and motor weakness in a cancer patient signal potential spinal cord compression, which causes permanent paralysis if untreated. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h3)

question: What absolute neutrophil count threshold defines severe neutropenia?

options.A: Between 1,000 and 2,500 cells per cubic millimeter
options.B: Below 500 cells per cubic millimeter
options.C: Above 20,000 cells per cubic millimeter
options.D: Between 5,000 and 10,000 cells per cubic millimeter

explanation: An absolute neutrophil count under 500 cells/mm³ leaves the body unable to fight off basic bacterial and fungal invasions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why is a fever in a neutropenic cancer patient treated as a medical emergency?

options.A: Fever always indicates that the primary cancer is spreading rapidly
options.B: Elevated body temperature immediately destroys remaining red blood cells
options.C: Antibiotics are ineffective once the patient develops a mild fever
options.D: The absence of white cells masks normal signs of severe infection

explanation: Without neutrophils, patients cannot mount typical inflammatory responses, meaning minor infections can quickly turn into fatal sepsis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is a common pitfall when assessing a patient undergoing cancer treatment?

options.A: Documenting intake and output with excessive and unnecessary detail
options.B: Performing vital signs checks too frequently throughout the day
options.C: Attributing early emergency symptoms to normal treatment side effects
options.D: Focusing exclusively on respiratory rates while ignoring the skin

explanation: Writing off subtle confusion or pain as expected fatigue can delay life-saving interventions for acute complications. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which parameter must be closely monitored to detect early renal compromise in tumor lysis syndrome?

options.A: Urine output and fluid balance
options.B: Body mass index and weight
options.C: Superficial skin turgor and moisture
options.D: Peripheral capillary refill time

explanation: Tracking urine output helps nurses spot acute kidney injury caused by uric acid crystal deposits in renal tubules. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h5)

question: How quickly should broad-spectrum antibiotics be administered for suspected febrile neutropenia?

options.A: Only after fever reaches 40 degrees Celsius
options.B: Within twelve hours of lab confirmation
options.C: Within one hour of presentation
options.D: Within twenty-four hours after culture results

explanation: Prompt antibiotic administration within the golden hour is critical to prevent septic shock in immunocompromised patients. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h6)

question: A patient with severe hypercalcemia of malignancy requires which initial medical therapy?

options.A: Intravenous normal saline and bisphosphonates
options.B: Immediate blood transfusion of packed cells
options.C: Oral potassium supplements and strict fluid restriction
options.D: High-protein diet and prolonged bed rest

explanation: Hydration flushes excess calcium through the kidneys, while bisphosphonates slow down bone resorption to lower blood calcium levels. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the term for programmed cell death regulated by the body?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Apoptosis
options.C: Hypertrophy
options.D: Necrosis

explanation: Apoptosis is the controlled process the body uses to eliminate damaged or unneeded cells safely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why are cell cycle checkpoints vital for normal tissue health?

options.A: They speed up the rate of tissue healing
options.B: They increase the size of aging cells
options.C: They supply extra blood to active tissues
options.D: They stop cells from dividing with damaged DNA

explanation: Checkpoints halt the cell cycle to allow for DNA repair or trigger cell death if damage is severe. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which feature is most characteristic of a benign tumor?

options.A: Presence of a capsule
options.B: Infiltration of nearby tissue
options.C: Spread to distant organs
options.D: Rapid, chaotic cell division

explanation: Benign tumors are typically enclosed within a fibrous capsule that keeps them localized. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: A biopsy report shows poorly differentiated cells with irregular borders. What does this mean?

options.A: A malignant neoplasm with invasive traits
options.B: A benign growth healing from chronic inflammation
options.C: Normal tissue regeneration after injury
options.D: A slow-growing encapsulated tissue mass

explanation: Poor differentiation and irregular borders are hallmark signs of malignancy and tissue invasion. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What happens when a proto-oncogene undergoes a mutation?

options.A: It triggers immediate programmed cell death
options.B: It becomes an oncogene that promotes rapid cell growth
options.C: It halts all protein synthesis in the cell
options.D: It transforms into a tumor suppressor gene

explanation: Mutations convert normal proto-oncogenes into overactive oncogenes that drive cancer development. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: How do tumor suppressor genes normally protect the human body?

options.A: By stimulating new blood vessel growth to injured areas
options.B: By slowing cell division and repairing damaged DNA
options.C: By speeding up the transport of nutrients into cells
options.D: By producing antibodies against abnormal proteins

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes act as molecular brakes to prevent uncontrolled cellular proliferation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: What occurs during the initiation phase of carcinogenesis?

options.A: New blood vessels form to feed the mass
options.B: Tumor cells spread to distant lymph nodes
options.C: The immune system destroys the mutated cells
options.D: Permanent DNA damage occurs in a cell

explanation: Initiation involves irreversible genetic damage caused by exposure to a carcinogen. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why is the promotion phase of cancer development considered reversible?

options.A: Removing the promoting stimulus can slow down repeated cell division
options.B: The body clears out all altered cells through normal digestion
options.C: Initiated cells automatically repair their DNA during this time
options.D: Immune responses permanently eliminate the tumor mass

explanation: Promotion relies on continuous exposure to growth stimuli, which can sometimes be reduced or stopped. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of tumor angiogenesis?

options.A: To shrink the overall size of the malignant lesion
options.B: To supply oxygen and nutrients to the growing mass
options.C: To remove waste products away from healthy tissue
options.D: To transport immune cells directly into the tumor core

explanation: Angiogenesis creates new blood vessels necessary to sustain the metabolic needs of a growing tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which chemical signal stimulates new vessel growth in tumors?

options.A: Insulin-like growth hormone
options.B: Erythropoietin stimulating factor
options.C: Vascular endothelial growth factor
options.D: C-reactive protein marker

explanation: Tumor cells secrete vascular endothelial growth factor to signal nearby blood vessels to sprout branches. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: What enzymes do cancer cells use to break through the extracellular matrix during invasion?

options.A: Insulin and glucagon
options.B: Matrix metalloproteinases
options.C: Amylase and lipase
options.D: Pepsin and trypsin

explanation: Matrix metalloproteinases degrade structural proteins in the extracellular matrix, clearing a path for tumor invasion. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the term for cancer cells entering local blood or lymphatic vessels?

options.A: Intravasation
options.B: Apoptosis
options.C: Extravasation
options.D: Angiogenesis

explanation: Intravasation describes cancer cells breaching vessel walls to enter the circulatory system. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which cells are primarily responsible for destroying abnormal and cancerous cells in the body?

options.A: Erythrocytes and platelets
options.B: Basophils and eosinophils
options.C: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes
options.D: Megakaryocytes

explanation: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes play a key role in cell-mediated immunity by targeting and destroying malignant cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: How do some tumor cells avoid being destroyed by the immune system?

options.A: By speeding up the normal metabolic rate of the liver
options.B: By forming a thick outer capsule made of red blood cells
options.C: By downregulating their abnormal surface antigens
options.D: By increasing their production of normal body hormones

explanation: Reducing or altering surface antigens prevents immune cells from recognizing the cancer as foreign. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the main event that starts the cancer process in a cell?

options.A: Complete cessation of cellular division
options.B: Shrinkage of tissue mass due to necrosis
options.C: Permanent DNA mutation in a cell
options.D: Rapid increase in normal cell apoptosis

explanation: Carcinogenesis begins when a normal cell undergoes a permanent change in its genetic material, often triggered by a carcinogen. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: How do cancer cells behave differently from normal cells during cell division?

options.A: Cancer cells rely entirely on external hormones to stimulate division
options.B: Cancer cells maintain strict control over their rate of growth
options.C: Cancer cells undergo apoptosis much faster than healthy cells
options.D: Cancer cells ignore signals to stop dividing and evade programmed cell death

explanation: Uncontrolled growth happens because cancer cells bypass normal body signals that tell them when to stop dividing and when to die. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which vaccine directly helps prevent cervical cancer?

options.A: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.B: Tetanus toxoid vaccine
options.C: Bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccine
options.D: Human Papillomavirus vaccine

explanation: The HPV vaccine protects against the high-risk viral strains that are the leading cause of cervical cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main goal of primary cancer prevention?

options.A: Preventing the initial onset of disease by reducing exposure to risk factors
options.B: Treating existing tumors to prevent metastasis to other organs
options.C: Detecting malignant tumors early through routine laboratory screening
options.D: Providing palliative care for patients in advanced disease stages

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping cancer before it starts by helping people avoid known risk factors. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which activity is an example of secondary cancer prevention?

options.A: Providing pain relief and comfort care in the terminal phase
options.B: Screening asymptomatic individuals to detect early-stage disease
options.C: Administering chemotherapy to shrink a confirmed metastatic tumor
options.D: Educating youth on the dangers of smoking cigarettes

explanation: Secondary prevention aims to catch cancer early in people who have no symptoms, which makes treatment more successful. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the difference between screening tests and diagnostic tests?

options.A: Screening is reserved for terminal patients, while diagnostics are for prevention
options.B: Screening is done on people without symptoms, while diagnostics investigate active complaints
options.C: Screening provides a definitive final diagnosis, while diagnostics are purely experimental
options.D: Screening is performed exclusively using blood work, while diagnostics use imaging

explanation: Screening checks healthy people for hidden signs of illness, whereas diagnostic tests find out why a sick person is having symptoms. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why is Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) often used for cervical screening in Nigerian primary health centers?

options.A: It is affordable, fast, and does not require complex laboratory equipment
options.B: It replaces the need for any future healthcare provider consultations
options.C: It is the only method recognized globally for definitive cancer staging
options.D: It provides a permanent genetic profile of the cervical tissue cells

explanation: VIA works well in settings with limited resources because it gives quick results without needing advanced laboratory machines. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: A 45-year-old Nigerian woman visits a primary health clinic feeling completely healthy. Which screening combination is most appropriate for her?

options.A: An immediate surgical biopsy of the breast and pelvic ultrasound
options.B: A full body magnetic resonance imaging scan and tumor marker panel
options.C: Chest X-ray and a sputum culture for malignant cells
options.D: Clinical breast examination and cervical screening via VIA or Pap smear

explanation: Breast and cervical cancers are the most common cancers among women in Nigeria, making routine checks for these two a priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: What does the letter 'T' stand for in the CAUTION warning signs of cancer?

options.A: Temperature elevation during evening hours
options.B: Tremors in the upper and lower extremities
options.C: Thickening or lump in the breast or elsewhere
options.D: Total loss of appetite and body weight

explanation: In the CAUTION reminder list, the letter T stands for any unusual thickening or lump found on the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why do cancer patients often experience unexplained weight loss and severe fatigue?

options.A: They prove that the patient is responding well to initial chemotherapy regimens
options.B: They indicate that the patient is consuming too many essential nutrients daily
options.C: They reflect the metabolic demands and inflammatory response triggered by a growing tumor
options.D: They are harmless side effects of normal aging processes in adults

explanation: Growing tumors use up a lot of the body's energy and release chemicals that change metabolism, causing severe weight loss and tiredness. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which procedure is necessary to give a definitive diagnosis of cancer?

options.A: Complete blood count with differential
options.B: Tissue biopsy and pathological examination
options.C: Routine digital rectal examination
options.D: Ultrasound scan of the abdomen

explanation: Scans and blood tests can suggest cancer, but looking at a tissue sample under a microscope is the only way to confirm it. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Rate of metabolic activity in regional lymph nodes
options.B: Total mass and weight of the primary tumor
options.C: Number of mitotic cells visible per microscope field
options.D: Presence of distant metastasis in other body organs

explanation: The M in TNM stands for metastasis, which tells us if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: How should nurses help address cultural myths about cancer during community health talks?

options.A: By discouraging patients from seeking formal medical evaluations in hospitals
options.B: By keeping all cancer diagnoses strictly secret from family members
options.C: By advising patients to rely solely on traditional herbal remedies for a cure
options.D: By providing accurate health education and encouraging early reporting of symptoms

explanation: Nurses help communities by replacing false beliefs with clear facts and encouraging people to visit the hospital early. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: A patient is afraid to get a biopsy because they believe cutting into a tumor makes it spread. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Tell the patient that their fear is unfounded and scold them for being uncooperative
options.B: Agree with the patient and cancel the scheduled procedure immediately
options.C: Document that the patient refuses care without offering further explanation
options.D: Explain the biopsy purpose calmly and correct the misconception using simple language

explanation: Nurses should listen to patient concerns and clear up common myths with gentle, easy-to-understand education. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary cellular change that initiates cancer development?

options.A: Rapid cell death caused by bacterial infections
options.B: Normal replacement of aging cells by healthy tissue
options.C: Uncontrolled cell multiplication due to genetic mutations
options.D: Permanent shrinkage of tissues due to poor blood supply

explanation: Cancer starts when genetic changes cause cells to divide uncontrollably and form abnormal masses. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why is the initial diagnostic phase particularly stressful for patients?

options.A: Hospital discharge planners force patients to relocate permanently
options.B: Treatment medications cause immediate physical weakness and hair loss
options.C: Diagnostic procedures require prolonged confinement in isolation wards
options.D: Patients face uncertainty and fear regarding potential outcomes

explanation: The suspicion of a life-threatening illness creates significant emotional turmoil and anxiety for the patient and family. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h1)

question: The main goal of cancer screening programs in healthy populations is to...

options.A: prevent all future genetic mutations
options.B: lower the financial cost of hospital care
options.C: detect malignancies before symptoms appear
options.D: cure advanced stages without surgery

explanation: Screening is designed to catch cancer early when treatment is most effective. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h2)

question: A patient scheduled for an endoscopic evaluation of the upper gastrointestinal tract needs nursing preparation that includes...

options.A: administering a high-protein meal before the test
options.B: ensuring the patient walks actively for two hours
options.C: restricting all oral fluids for exactly one week
options.D: verifying informed consent and fasting status

explanation: Endoscopic procedures require an empty stomach to ensure clear visualization and prevent aspiration risks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h2)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Mitotic rate
options.B: Distant metastasis
options.C: Microscopic size
options.D: Malignant mass

explanation: In TNM staging, M indicates whether the cancer has spread to distant organs in the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h3)

question: How does a Grade 4 tumor differ functionally from a Grade 1 tumor?

options.A: Grade 4 growths respond instantly to mild dietary changes
options.B: Grade 4 cells look highly abnormal and multiply rapidly
options.C: Grade 4 tumors never spread beyond the local tissue site
options.D: Grade 4 cells resemble normal healthy tissue very closely

explanation: Higher tumor grades indicate poorly differentiated, aggressive cells that grow and spread quickly. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is a tissue biopsy considered essential in cancer diagnosis?

options.A: It provides definitive microscopic proof of malignancy
options.B: It completely cures the patient without further drugs
options.C: It replaces the need for any blood investigations
options.D: It eliminates all post-operative pain immediately

explanation: Only direct examination of cellular tissue by a pathologist can definitively confirm the presence of cancer cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h4)

question: Immediately after obtaining a surgical tissue specimen, the nurse must...

options.A: store it inside a standard household refrigerator overnight
options.B: leave the specimen exposed to air on the procedure tray
options.C: wash the tissue sample thoroughly with sterile tap water
options.D: place it in the proper fixative solution and label it accurately

explanation: Proper fixation prevents tissue degradation and accurate labeling prevents dangerous diagnostic mix-ups. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h4)

question: Which nursing action is most critical immediately following a liver biopsy?

options.A: Administering a large oral dose of routine laxatives
options.B: Placing a hot water bottle directly over the puncture site
options.C: Encouraging immediate ambulation around the hospital ward
options.D: Positioning the patient on the right side to apply pressure

explanation: Lying on the right side helps tamponade the liver capsule against the abdominal wall to minimize bleeding risks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h5)

question: A common post-procedural complication that nurses must monitor for after a core needle biopsy is...

options.A: sudden enlargement of skeletal bones
options.B: internal or external hemorrhage
options.C: permanent loss of memory function
options.D: complete cessation of urine production

explanation: Because biopsies disrupt tissue and blood vessels, bleeding is a primary risk that requires vigilant monitoring. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h5)

question: How can a nurse best help a patient experiencing severe anxiety while waiting for biopsy results?

options.A: Reassure the patient firmly that the laboratory results will be normal
options.B: Provide a quiet, supportive environment and listen attentively to fears
options.C: Advise the patient to avoid asking questions about the disease
options.D: Keep the patient heavily sedated until the final report arrives

explanation: Active listening and calm reassurance validate patient feelings without making false promises about medical outcomes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h6)

question: A physical sign that frequently accompanies high levels of diagnostic-related anxiety is...

options.A: persistent insomnia and elevated heart rate
options.B: profound slowing of the resting pulse rate
options.C: sudden increase in normal daily appetite
options.D: extreme muscle relaxation and deep sleep

explanation: Anxiety activates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to physiological symptoms like tachycardia and sleep disturbances. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team approach essential in the management of newly diagnosed cancer?

options.A: It removes the need for nurses to communicate with the patient family
options.B: It allows the hospital administration to reduce total nursing staff numbers
options.C: It ensures that surgical procedures are performed without any assistance
options.D: It combines diverse expert knowledge to create a comprehensive treatment plan

explanation: Cancer care is complex, requiring input from doctors, nurses, and specialists to address all aspects of the disease. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: A primary responsibility of the oncology nurse within the multidisciplinary team is to...

options.A: coordinate patient care and bridge communication between specialists
options.B: perform independent pathological analysis of tissue slides
options.C: make the final decision regarding chemotherapy drug dosages
options.D: prescribe specialized radiological scans for staging purposes

explanation: Nurses spend the most time with patients, placing them in the ideal position to coordinate care and relay information. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T4#GNS321_U1_T4_h7)

question: In which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication take place?

options.A: G1 phase
options.B: S phase
options.C: M phase
options.D: G2 phase

explanation: During the synthesis or S phase, the cell replicates its entire genome to ensure each daughter cell receives a complete set of chromosomes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the primary function of checkpoints in the cell cycle?

options.A: To force cells into permanent cell death
options.B: To halt division if DNA damage is detected
options.C: To double the number of chromosomes in a cell
options.D: To speed up the rate of protein synthesis

explanation: Checkpoints act as quality control mechanisms that pause the cycle to allow for DNA repair before replication or division continues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which term describes the reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another?

options.A: Metaplasia
options.B: Anaplasia
options.C: Hyperplasia
options.D: Dysplasia

explanation: Metaplasia occurs when chronic stress causes one adult cell type to adapt by changing into another adult cell type suited to survive the stress. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: Why is dysplasia considered clinically significant for nursing and medical care?

options.A: It represents completely normal tissue aging
options.B: It serves as a recognized precancerous condition
options.C: It always results in immediate organ failure
options.D: It indicates that cells have reverted to normal function

explanation: Dysplastic changes show disordered growth and loss of uniformity, which frequently progress to malignancy if the triggering stimulus is not removed. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is a key characteristic of benign tumors?

options.A: They consist of poorly differentiated cells
options.B: They are usually encapsulated and localized
options.C: They frequently spread to distant organs
options.D: They invade surrounding blood vessels

explanation: Benign tumors possess a fibrous capsule that keeps them contained, preventing local tissue invasion and distant metastasis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: How do malignant tumors primarily differ from benign growths in terms of tissue effect?

options.A: Malignant tumors invade surrounding structures and metastasize
options.B: Malignant tumors grow significantly slower than benign tumors
options.C: Malignant tumors always remain within their original organ
options.D: Malignant tumors never cause disruption to normal physiology

explanation: The defining trait of malignancy is the ability to break through basement membranes, invade adjacent tissue, and travel through blood and lymphatics. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h3)

question: What defines a multipotent stem cell?

options.A: It can only divide once before undergoing necrosis
options.B: It can differentiate into a limited range of cell types
options.C: It has lost all capacity for further cell division
options.D: It can form every cell type in the human body

explanation: Multipotent stem cells are restricted to giving rise to cell types within a particular family, such as blood cells arising from bone marrow stem cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: What happens during asymmetric division of a normal stem cell?

options.A: The cell divides without replicating its genetic material
options.B: Both daughter cells undergo rapid programmed cell death
options.C: One daughter cell remains a stem cell and the other differentiates
options.D: Both daughter cells immediately differentiate into mature tissue

explanation: Asymmetric division preserves the essential stem cell reservoir while simultaneously supplying new cells for tissue maintenance and repair. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is the normal function of a proto-oncogene in the human body?

options.A: To repair damaged segments of DNA strands
options.B: To promote normal cell growth and proliferation
options.C: To destroy abnormal extracellular proteins
options.D: To induce immediate programmed cell death

explanation: Proto-oncogenes code for proteins that stimulate cell division and development, becoming dangerous only when mutated into hyperactive oncogenes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: How do mutated tumor suppressor genes contribute to cancer development?

options.A: By preventing cells from entering the G0 resting phase
options.B: By increasing the production of protective hormones
options.C: By accelerating the repair of all cellular mutations
options.D: By removing cellular checks and allowing uncontrolled growth

explanation: When tumor suppressor genes lose their function, the cell loses critical inhibitory controls, making unregulated proliferation much more likely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which enzymes are primarily responsible for executing apoptosis within the cell?

options.A: Histones
options.B: Caspases
options.C: Amylases
options.D: Lipases

explanation: Caspases are a family of protease enzymes that activate in a cascade to systematically dismantle cellular components during apoptosis. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: How does apoptosis fundamentally differ from necrosis in tissue injury?

options.A: Apoptosis only affects red blood cells, whereas necrosis affects bone
options.B: Apoptosis requires no cellular energy, whereas necrosis requires ATP
options.C: Apoptosis is a regulated, programmed process, whereas necrosis is accidental
options.D: Apoptosis causes severe inflammation, whereas necrosis does not

explanation: Programmed cell death is orderly and clean, packaged into apoptotic bodies, whereas necrosis involves cell lysis, spilling contents and causing inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why do conventional chemotherapy drugs frequently cause hair loss and mouth sores?

options.A: They target rapidly dividing healthy mucosal and hair cells
options.B: They specifically target the nervous system receptors
options.C: They disrupt the normal blood supply to the skin
options.D: They permanently destroy all dormant stem cell reserves

explanation: Traditional chemotherapy drugs affect any rapidly proliferating cells in the body, which includes healthy mucosal linings and hair follicles alongside cancer cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: A patient receiving chemotherapy presents with low white blood cell counts. What is the primary nursing priority?

options.A: Encouraging vigorous physical exercise to boost bone marrow function
options.B: Monitoring strictly for signs of infection and implementing precautions
options.C: Preparing the patient for immediate radiation therapy sessions
options.D: Administering high-dose topical treatments for potential skin rashes

explanation: Myelosuppression reduces white blood cells, leaving the patient vulnerable to opportunistic infections, making infection prevention the top clinical priority. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T5#GNS321_U1_T5_h7)

question: What does the medical term neoplasm mean?

options.A: Cell shrinkage
options.B: Normal healing
options.C: Tissue infection
options.D: New growth

explanation: Neoplasm translates directly to new growth, describing the unregulated multiplication of cells within the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why does neoplastic tissue continue to grow after the original trigger stops?

options.A: Cellular control mechanisms have failed completely
options.B: The body demands extra energy for daily tasks
options.C: Normal healing requires permanent cell enlargement
options.D: Local blood supply decreases over time

explanation: Uncontrolled growth happens because mutations disrupt the normal signals that tell cells when to stop dividing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which feature is typical of benign tumor cells?

options.A: Capable of traveling through lymphatic channels
options.B: Poorly differentiated and rapidly spreading
options.C: Well-differentiated and resemble original tissue
options.D: Non-encapsulated with irregular borders

explanation: Benign cells retain characteristics of the tissue they originated from and stay confined locally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the main danger of a benign brain tumor?

options.A: Destroying distant lymph nodes
options.B: Compression of surrounding vital brain tissue
options.C: Spreading rapidly to the lungs and liver
options.D: Releasing widespread systemic toxins

explanation: Even though benign cells do not spread to other parts of the body, their physical expansion inside a rigid skull can damage critical brain structures. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h2)

question: What type of tissue gives rise to a carcinoma?

options.A: Connective tissue
options.B: Lymphatic tissue
options.C: Muscle tissue
options.D: Epithelial tissue

explanation: Carcinomas develop from the cells that line the surfaces, cavities, and organs of the body, which are epithelial tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: A tumor arising from bone and cartilage tissue is best classified as a:

options.A: Carcinoma
options.B: Lymphoma
options.C: Sarcoma
options.D: Leukemia

explanation: Sarcomas originate from connective tissues such as bone, cartilage, fat, and muscle. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h3)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Microscopic grading
options.B: Distant metastasis
options.C: Mitotic rate
options.D: Malignant mass

explanation: The M category in TNM staging indicates whether the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why is cancer grading important for treatment planning?

options.A: It measures how aggressive and abnormal the tumor cells appear microscopically
options.B: It determines the patient's exact geographical location for follow-up
options.C: It counts the number of lymph nodes involved in the disease process
options.D: It tracks the exact physical size of the tumor inside the organ

explanation: Grading focuses on cellular appearance under a microscope, giving clues about how fast the tumor is likely to grow. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h4)

question: A chemotherapy patient has a low neutrophil count. What is the most important infection control action for the nurse?

options.A: Place the patient in a standard open ward bed
options.B: Administer live vaccines to boost immunity immediately
options.C: Enforce strict hand hygiene and limit visitor exposure
options.D: Encourage consumption of fresh salads and raw fruits

explanation: Patients with low neutrophil counts have compromised immune defenses, making rigorous infection control measures vital for safety. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of monitoring platelet counts during cancer chemotherapy?

options.A: To assess the patient's nutritional status
options.B: To measure the exact size of the solid tumor
options.C: To detect and prevent bleeding risks
options.D: To evaluate the patient's daily fluid intake

explanation: Platelets are essential for blood clotting, and low counts caused by bone marrow suppression put the patient at risk for bleeding. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T6#GNS321_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the term for cells in a malignant tumor that completely lose their normal features and differentiation?

options.A: Hyperplasia
options.B: Anaplasia
options.C: Dysplasia
options.D: Metaplasia

explanation: Anaplasia refers to poorly differentiated cells that lose their mature functions and begin to look like primitive, unspecialized cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why is dysplasia more worrying for cancer development than simple hyperplasia?

options.A: Hyperplasia only occurs in response to chronic bacterial infections
options.B: Hyperplasia cells always immediately invade surrounding basement membranes
options.C: Dysplasia stops blood supply from reaching the affected tissue
options.D: Dysplasia involves disordered cell growth with abnormal shape and size

explanation: Dysplasia shows abnormal changes in how cells are organized, sized, and shaped, making it a stronger warning sign for potential cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which structure is typically found around a benign tumor, helping to keep it contained?

options.A: A fibrous capsule
options.B: An extensive vascular network
options.C: Undifferentiated stem cells
options.D: Metastatic secondary lesions

explanation: Benign tumors usually grow inside a clear fibrous capsule, which stops them from spreading into nearby healthy tissues. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What makes a benign brain tumor dangerous even though it is non-cancerous?

options.A: Spreading malignant cells through the cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Releasing systemic toxins into the bloodstream
options.C: Triggering widespread immune system collapse
options.D: Compression of vital surrounding neural structures

explanation: Because the skull has fixed space, even a non-cancerous tumor can grow, raise pressure inside the head, and damage delicate brain tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is the normal job of a proto-oncogene in a healthy cell?

options.A: To promote normal cellular growth and division
options.B: To form a protective fibrous capsule around organs
options.C: To trigger immediate apoptosis in aged cells
options.D: To repair damaged DNA strands inside the nucleus

explanation: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that help regulate and encourage healthy cell growth and division. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: What happens when both copies of a tumor suppressor gene are damaged or turned off?

options.A: The immune system destroys the affected tissue
options.B: DNA replication stops permanently in all body tissues
options.C: The cell immediately transforms into a benign cyst
options.D: The cell loses its normal control over division

explanation: Tumor suppressor genes act like brakes on cell growth. Losing both copies removes this control, allowing cells to divide uncontrollably. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h3)

question: During which step of cancer development does the first permanent damage to DNA happen?

options.A: Initiation
options.B: Metastasis
options.C: Promotion
options.D: Progression

explanation: Initiation happens when a cell is exposed to something that causes permanent genetic damage. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why is rapid cell division during the promotion stage important for cancer to develop?

options.A: It immediately triggers the development of a fibrous capsule
options.B: It activates the immune system to destroy the tumor
options.C: It increases the population of cells harboring mutations
options.D: It repairs damaged DNA strands before progression starts

explanation: Promotion encourages cells to divide, building up a larger group of mutated cells that are more likely to develop further cancerous changes. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h4)

question: Which chemical factor is mainly responsible for telling new blood vessels to grow inside a tumor?

options.A: Epithelial Cadherin Molecule
options.B: Tumor Suppressor Protein
options.C: Fibrous Collagen Matrix
options.D: Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor

explanation: VEGF is a signal released by oxygen-starved tumor cells that tricks nearby blood vessels into sprouting new branches toward the tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why do growing tumors need to build new blood vessels once they pass a microscopic size?

options.A: New blood vessels are needed to produce a protective capsule
options.B: The host immune system blocks normal cellular fluid exchange
options.C: Nutrients inside the cell cytoplasm become completely depleted
options.D: Diffusion alone cannot supply enough oxygen and nutrients

explanation: Oxygen and nutrients can only pass short distances through tissue by simple movement, so tumors must grow their own blood supply to keep getting food and air. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which enzyme do cancer cells use to break down surrounding tissue barriers during local spread?

options.A: Epithelial cadherin molecules
options.B: Vascular endothelial growth factors
options.C: Cellular proto-oncogenes
options.D: Matrix metalloproteinases

explanation: MMPs are enzymes released by cancer cells to chew through structural barriers like basement membranes and connective tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the main effect of losing epithelial cadherin in cancer cells?

options.A: It protects circulating tumor cells from host immune attack
options.B: It reduces cell-to-cell adhesion, allowing cells to break away
options.C: It halts uncontrolled cell division within the core of the mass
options.D: It stimulates rapid angiogenesis around the primary tumor site

explanation: E-cadherin acts like glue holding cells to their neighbors. Losing it allows individual cancer cells to let go and travel elsewhere. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the term for the severe muscle wasting and weight loss often seen in people with advanced cancer?

options.A: Metastatic dissemination
options.B: Cellular anaplasia
options.C: Cancer cachexia
options.D: Paraneoplastic syndrome

explanation: Cachexia is a body-wide wasting syndrome involving rapid muscle breakdown and altered metabolism triggered by tumor-related inflammation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: How do paraneoplastic syndromes usually happen in cancer patients?

options.A: Metastatic lesions completely destroy the liver and kidneys
options.B: Tumor cells secrete ectopic hormones or immune-triggering peptides
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs directly damage the central nervous system
options.D: Mechanical pressure from the primary tumor blocks endocrine glands

explanation: Paraneoplastic syndromes occur because cancer cells release abnormal hormones or chemicals that affect normal tissues far away from the tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T7#GNS321_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary objective of cancer treatment aimed at complete eradication?

options.A: Control
options.B: Cure
options.C: Palliations
options.D: Prevention

explanation: A cure means the complete eradication of the malignant disease to restore normal life expectancy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: A patient with widespread metastasis receives care focused solely on comfort and symptom relief. Which treatment goal does this describe?

options.A: Control
options.B: Prophylaxis
options.C: Palliations
options.D: Cure

explanation: Palliative care focuses on relieving symptoms and maximizing comfort when the disease cannot be cured. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: Removing a non-vital organ to prevent future cancer development is known as which type of surgery?

options.A: Prophylactic surgery
options.B: Curative resection
options.C: Diagnostic biopsy
options.D: Palliative surgery

explanation: Prophylactic surgery involves removing at-risk healthy tissue to prevent a malignancy from developing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why is a wide margin of healthy tissue removed during a curative cancer surgery?

options.A: To promote faster healing of the surgical wound site
options.B: To ensure microscopic cancer cells left behind are excised
options.C: To prevent the patient from experiencing postoperative pain
options.D: To eliminate the need for any subsequent radiation therapy

explanation: Removing a rim of normal tissue helps guarantee that all microscopic extensions of the tumor are removed. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is the term for radiation therapy delivered via implanted radioactive sources close to the tumor?

options.A: Brachytherapy
options.B: Chemotherapy
options.C: Teletherapy
options.D: Immunotherapy

explanation: Brachytherapy involves placing radioactive material directly inside or adjacent to the tumor site. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: A nurse is teaching skin care to a patient receiving external radiation. Which instruction is appropriate to include?

options.A: Wash the marked area gently with mild soap and water
options.B: Scrub the treatment markings vigorously during your daily bath
options.C: Apply heating pads to the skin area to relieve local muscle ache
options.D: Use adhesive medical tape firmly to secure dressings over the site

explanation: Gentle washing protects fragile irradiated skin from breakdown, while friction, heat, and adhesive tapes should be avoided. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary hazard when a vesicant chemotherapy drug leaks into surrounding subcutaneous tissue?

options.A: Transient skin pigmentation
options.B: Severe tissue necrosis
options.C: Rapid bone marrow recovery
options.D: Immediate systemic cure

explanation: Vesicants are agents that blister and destroy tissue, leading to severe localized necrosis if extravasation occurs. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: What action should a nurse take first when suspecting an intravenous chemotherapy extravasation?

options.A: Document the event at the end of the shift
options.B: Apply firm pressure to the site
options.C: Stop the infusion immediately
options.D: Flush the line with normal saline

explanation: Stopping the infusion prevents any further vesicant medication from entering the subcutaneous tissue. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: How do targeted therapies differ from traditional systemic chemotherapy drugs?

options.A: They work exclusively by increasing red blood cell counts
options.B: They destroy all rapidly dividing cells in the human body
options.C: They only affect patients with localized skin malignancies
options.D: They focus on specific molecular characteristics of cancer cells

explanation: Targeted therapies are designed to interfere with specific molecules needed for tumor growth rather than non-specifically targeting all dividing cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which mechanism describes how immune checkpoint inhibitors work in cancer treatment?

options.A: They lower systemic inflammation to keep the patient comfortable
options.B: They directly replace damaged bone marrow cells after high-dose radiation
options.C: They coat the exterior of solid tumors to prevent blood vessel growth
options.D: They help the patient immune system recognize and attack cancer cells

explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors remove molecular brakes on immune cells, allowing T-cells to mount an attack against the tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which oncological emergency features facial edema, jugular venous distension, and respiratory distress?

options.A: Spinal Cord Compression
options.B: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
options.C: Hypercalcemia of Malignancy
options.D: Tumor Lysis Syndrome

explanation: Compression of the superior vena cava impairs venous return from the upper body, causing characteristic facial and neck swelling. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary physiological cause of electrolyte imbalances in Tumor Lysis Syndrome?

options.A: Rapid destruction of large numbers of tumor cells
options.B: Kidney failure caused by radiation therapy to the pelvis
options.C: Excessive dietary intake of potassium during chemotherapy
options.D: Dehydration from severe chemotherapy-induced nausea

explanation: TLS occurs when massive cell breakdown releases intracellular contents like potassium and phosphate rapidly into the circulation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary framework used to guide pharmacological cancer pain management?

options.A: TNM cancer staging classification system
options.B: World Health Organization analgesic ladder
options.C: ECOG performance status evaluation tool
options.D: Glasgow Coma Scale neurological assessment

explanation: The WHO analgesic ladder provides a stepwise approach for prescribing pain medications based on pain severity. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: A patient receiving emetogenic chemotherapy asks when to take their prescribed antiemetic medication. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Wait until you feel severe nausea before taking the first dose
options.B: Only take the medication if you actually vomit twice
options.C: Take it proactively before the chemotherapy session starts
options.D: Take it strictly at bedtime regardless of your treatment schedule

explanation: Prophylactic antiemetic administration is much more effective at preventing chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting than rescue treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: When should palliative care ideally be introduced in the cancer care continuum?

options.A: Exclusively when the patient is discharged to hospice
options.B: After all forms of chemotherapy have failed
options.C: Only during the final forty-eight hours of life
options.D: Integrated early alongside active disease-directed treatments

explanation: Early integration of palliative care improves quality of life and symptom management throughout the disease trajectory. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of palliative care for a patient with advanced cancer?

options.A: Shrinking tumor size through high-dose radiation therapy
options.B: Finding a definitive cure for the underlying malignancy
options.C: Improving quality of life for both patient and family
options.D: Preventing the development of secondary infections

explanation: Palliative care prioritizes comfort, symptom management, and psychosocial support rather than disease eradication. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the main goal of palliative care in cancer treatment?

options.A: Stimulate rapid cellular regeneration
options.B: Cure the primary malignancy completely
options.C: Prevent secondary genetic mutations
options.D: Relieving symptoms and improving comfort

explanation: Palliative care focuses on relieving distress and enhancing the quality of life rather than curing the disease. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why are systemic cancer therapies used instead of localized treatments when cancer has spread?

options.A: They act exclusively on localized solid tumors
options.B: They avoid all forms of systemic toxicity and adverse effects
options.C: They replace the need for surgical staging completely
options.D: They travel via the bloodstream to reach widespread malignant cells

explanation: Systemic medications circulate through the blood vessels, allowing them to reach cancer cells that have spread to different parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which waste container is used for discarded chemotherapy materials?

options.A: Puncture-proof green sharps boxes
options.B: Standard black household bins
options.C: Clear biodegradable refuse bags
options.D: Yellow cytotoxic waste containers

explanation: Special yellow containers are used for the safe disposal and incineration of hazardous cytotoxic waste. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h2)

question: A nurse spills an intravenous chemotherapy drug inside the safety cabinet. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Spray regular hospital disinfectant over the affected surface
options.B: Leave the hood running and wait for the maintenance team
options.C: Wipe the surface immediately with a standard dry paper towel
options.D: Use the designated chemotherapy spill kit to clean the area

explanation: Certified spill kits contain neutralizing agents and materials designed specifically to clean up hazardous drug spills safely. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h2)

question: How do targeted cancer therapies differ from traditional chemotherapy?

options.A: They focus on specific molecular features driving cancer cell growth
options.B: They require continuous infusion pumps rather than oral dosing
options.C: They work exclusively by boosting the patient's white blood cells
options.D: They destroy all rapidly dividing cells throughout the entire body

explanation: Targeted drugs zero in on precise proteins or genetic changes unique to cancer cells, unlike traditional chemotherapy which affects all fast-growing cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the main action of immune checkpoint inhibitors in cancer care?

options.A: Inhibiting the hormonal production of estrogen in female patients
options.B: Emitting localized ionizing radiation to shrink tumor blood vessels
options.C: Blocking proteins that prevent T-cells from attacking cancer cells
options.D: Directly replacing damaged bone marrow stem cells with donors

explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors remove the signals that hold back the immune system, allowing T-cells to attack the tumor. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which type of cancer is most commonly treated with hormone therapy?

options.A: Primary glioblastoma of the brain
options.B: Hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer
options.C: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
options.D: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

explanation: Hormones like estrogen can fuel certain breast cancers, so blocking these hormones is an effective treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is the main goal of hormone therapy in cancer treatment?

options.A: Enhance the replication rate of healthy endocrine glands
options.B: Lower hormone production or block receptors feeding the tumor
options.C: Replace damaged cellular DNA within the bone marrow
options.D: Stimulate systemic inflammatory responses against metastasis

explanation: Depriving hormone-dependent cancers of their growth signals helps slow or stop the disease from progressing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why are ink marks placed on the skin before external beam radiation therapy?

options.A: Guiding the surgeon during subsequent resections
options.B: Identifying areas of active bacterial skin infection
options.C: Mapping out sites for intravenous cannula insertion
options.D: Ensuring precise daily targeting of the tumor site

explanation: Skin markings ensure the radiation beam is directed to the exact same spot during every treatment session. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h5)

question: A patient receiving radiation to the neck asks if they can use scented lotion on the area. What should the nurse say?

options.A: Avoid perfumed lotions because they can irritate the sensitive skin
options.B: Rub the scented cream vigorously to enhance skin absorption
options.C: Use alcohol-based rubs instead to keep the skin sterile and dry
options.D: Apply the lotion heavily right before each radiation session begins

explanation: Fragrances and chemicals can worsen skin irritation and breakdown within the radiation treatment field. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h5)

question: What is the most reliable early sign of infection in a patient with neutropenia?

options.A: An elevated body temperature
options.B: A drop in blood pressure
options.C: Yellow discoloration of skin
options.D: Severe localized pain in joints

explanation: Because neutropenic patients have low white blood cells and may not show typical signs like pus or swelling, fever is often the only warning sign of infection. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h6)

question: Why is mouth care so important for a patient undergoing chemotherapy?

options.A: It prevents painful mucosal ulcerations and secondary infections
options.B: It stimulates the appetite by clearing leftover food debris
options.C: It maintains adequate salivary pH levels during dehydration
options.D: It stops systemic bone marrow suppression from worsening

explanation: Chemotherapy harms rapidly dividing cells in the mouth lining, making good oral hygiene vital to prevent severe sores and infection. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h6)

question: Which electrolyte imbalance is a classic sign of tumor lysis syndrome?

options.A: Hypokalemia
options.B: Hypercalcemia
options.C: Hyponatremia
options.D: Hyperkalemia

explanation: The rapid breakdown of cancer cells releases large amounts of potassium into the bloodstream, causing dangerous hyperkalemia. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h7)

question: What is an early warning sign of spinal cord compression in a cancer patient?

options.A: Throbbing headaches worse in the early morning
options.B: Intermittent cramping abdominal pain after meals
options.C: New onset back pain accompanied by motor weakness
options.D: Sharp chest pain radiating down the left arm

explanation: Tumor pressure on the spinal cord usually starts with back pain, followed by nerve problems like muscle weakness or numbness. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h7)

question: What preventive care is standard for a patient starting regular opioid pain medication?

options.A: Monitoring hourly urine output via a catheter
options.B: Administering prescribed stool softeners and laxatives
options.C: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload
options.D: Checking deep tendon reflexes every four hours

explanation: Opioids slow down bowel movements, so starting a bowel routine early is essential to prevent severe constipation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h8)

question: How does palliative care differ from curative treatment?

options.A: It is administered only after all chemotherapy regimens fail
options.B: It prioritizes comfort and symptom relief over disease eradication
options.C: It is restricted exclusively to the final 24 hours of life
options.D: It forbids the use of any medications that affect consciousness

explanation: Palliative care can be started at any point during a serious illness to ease suffering and improve quality of life, regardless of whether a cure is possible. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T9#GNS321_U1_T9_h8)

question: Who pioneered the practice of placing critically ill soldiers close to nursing stations?

options.A: Clara Barton
options.B: Mary Seacole
options.C: Florence Nightingale
options.D: Linda Richards

explanation: Florence Nightingale grouped the most severely wounded soldiers nearest the nursing station during the Crimean War to ensure close observation. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why did Florence Nightingale place critically ill patients near the nurses' station?

options.A: To limit the spread of airborne hospital infections
options.B: To ensure doctors could access them first
options.C: To provide continuous observation and care
options.D: To keep them away from noisy recovery wards

explanation: Grouping unstable patients near the nursing station allowed nurses to monitor them constantly and intervene rapidly when changes occurred. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which major disease outbreak drove the early development of mechanical ventilation?

options.A: Influenza
options.B: Cholera
options.C: Poliomyelitis
options.D: Tuberculosis

explanation: The polio epidemics of the mid-20th century caused widespread respiratory paralysis, which forced hospitals to develop mechanical ventilation methods. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h2)

question: What role did nursing play during the polio epidemics regarding respiratory support?

options.A: Manufacturing iron lung machines in hospital basements
options.B: Performing emergency spinal tap procedures on all admissions
options.C: Providing continuous manual ventilation and airway management
options.D: Prescribing muscle relaxants to ease breathing difficulties

explanation: Nurses worked around the clock performing manual ventilation and managing tracheostomies when mechanical iron lungs failed. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h2)

question: Where was the first centralized intensive care ward established during a polio outbreak?

options.A: London
options.B: Paris
options.C: New York
options.D: Copenhagen

explanation: The first centralized respiratory care ward was established in Copenhagen in 1953 by Bjorn Ibsen during a severe polio epidemic. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h3)

question: What was the main advantage of centralizing critically ill patients into one ward?

options.A: Eliminating the need for physician oversight during night shifts
options.B: Allowing families to visit patients without restriction
options.C: Reducing the overall cost of hospital construction and maintenance
options.D: Pooling specialized equipment and expert nursing staff in one location

explanation: Centralizing critical patients allowed hospitals to concentrate scarce resources like ventilators and specially trained nurses where they were needed most. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h3)

question: What specialized unit was created in the 1960s specifically for heart attack patients?

options.A: Neurological Trauma Unit
options.B: Cardiothoracic Recovery Ward
options.C: Surgical Intensive Care Unit
options.D: Coronary Care Unit

explanation: Coronary Care Units were established in the 1960s to monitor heart attack patients continuously and treat lethal arrhythmias immediately. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why did the introduction of coronary care units drastically reduce heart attack mortality?

options.A: High doses of intravenous antibiotics prevented secondary infections
options.B: Doctors developed surgical cures for blocked coronary arteries
options.C: Continuous ECG monitoring allowed immediate intervention for fatal arrhythmias
options.D: Patients were kept completely unconscious to rest their hearts

explanation: Continuous cardiac monitoring enabled nurses and doctors to catch ventricular fibrillation early and apply defibrillation before irreversible damage occurred. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h4)

question: When was the American Association of Critical-Care Nurses founded to formalize the specialty?
explanation: The AACN was founded in 1969 to set professional standards and provide formal education for nurses working in intensive care environments. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h5)

question: What drove the transformation of critical care nursing into a distinct formal specialty?

options.A: The desire of physicians to delegate all administrative paperwork
options.B: The demand from hospital administrators for lower staffing costs
options.C: The reduction in nursing school enrollment numbers worldwide
options.D: The complexity of advanced life support technology and monitoring systems

explanation: Advanced monitors, ventilators, and vasoactive medications required nurses to possess specialized physiological knowledge beyond basic general nursing training. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which device provides real-time, beat-to-beat blood pressure tracking in the ICU?

options.A: Central venous line
options.B: Standard sphygmomanometer
options.C: Arterial catheter
options.D: Pulse oximeter probe

explanation: An arterial catheter inserted into a peripheral artery provides continuous, beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring for unstable patients. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h6)

question: How do modern electronic health records improve patient safety in critical care units?

options.A: By automatically diagnosing complications before symptoms appear
options.B: By allowing family members to update patient charts from home
options.C: By integrating alarms, lab values, and medication orders into one system
options.D: By replacing the need for bedside physical assessments by nurses

explanation: Integrated digital systems help reduce medication and monitoring errors by centralizing critical patient data in real time. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is a primary focus for advancing critical care nursing practice in Nigeria today?

options.A: Eliminating the need for mechanical ventilators in emergency wards
options.B: Transitioning entirely to outpatient surgical care models
options.C: Replacing all bedside nurses with automated robotic systems
options.D: Expanding specialized training programs and improving resource management

explanation: Nigerian critical care development emphasizes specialized training and overcoming local resource challenges to improve patient survival rates. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h7)

question: How can artificial intelligence predictive analytics assist intensive care unit nurses?

options.A: By taking over direct physical patient hygiene and turning schedules
options.B: By alerting staff to clinical deterioration before overt symptoms appear
options.C: By discharging stable patients without requiring nursing sign-off
options.D: By replacing physician rounds with automated electronic prescriptions

explanation: Predictive analytics analyze continuous monitor data to warn nurses of complications like sepsis or shock hours ahead of time. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T1#GNS321_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of mechanical ventilation?

options.A: To prevent cardiac arrest in all patients
options.B: To cure primary lung diseases
options.C: To deliver oral medications directly to alveoli
options.D: To assist or replace spontaneous breathing

explanation: Mechanical ventilation acts as a supportive measure to handle gas exchange when the patient's respiratory system fails. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome develops respiratory muscle weakness. Why is mechanical ventilation needed?

options.A: To lower elevated systemic blood pressure
options.B: To correct metabolic alkalosis quickly
options.C: To manage impending respiratory failure
options.D: To prevent upper airway infections

explanation: Neuromuscular weakness impairs the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, making spontaneous breathing difficult and leading to respiratory failure. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: What does PEEP stand for in mechanical ventilation settings?

options.A: Peak emergency evacuation pressure
options.B: Primary endotracheal expulsion parameter
options.C: Positive end-expiratory pressure
options.D: Pulmonary evaluation and expansion protocol

explanation: PEEP maintains a baseline pressure above atmospheric pressure at the end of expiration to prevent alveolar collapse. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: Which ventilator mode allows the patient to breathe spontaneously between mandatory machine-delivered breaths?

options.A: Controlled Mandatory Ventilation
options.B: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
options.C: Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation
options.D: Inverse Ratio Ventilation

explanation: SIMV delivers preset mandatory breaths while letting the patient take spontaneous breaths in between, useful for weaning. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: How often should oral care with an antiseptic solution be performed for a ventilated patient?

options.A: Once every twelve hours
options.B: Every two to four hours
options.C: Once daily during the morning shift
options.D: Only when visible debris is present

explanation: Frequent oral care minimizes oral bacterial load, which is a primary risk factor for ventilator-associated pneumonia. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: A high-pressure alarm sounds on the mechanical ventilator. What is the immediate nursing action?

options.A: Increase the set tidal volume
options.B: Assess the patient and check the circuit for kinks or secretions
options.C: Extubate the patient immediately to restore natural breathing
options.D: Turn off the alarm permanently

explanation: High-pressure alarms indicate increased resistance or decreased compliance, requiring immediate physical assessment of both patient and machine. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the maximum recommended duration for a single pass of endotracheal suctioning?

options.A: Ten to fifteen seconds
options.B: Thirty to forty-five seconds
options.C: Two to three minutes
options.D: One minute exactly

explanation: Limiting suction time prevents severe hypoxemia and cardiac arrhythmias caused by oxygen deprivation during the procedure. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: Why is hyperoxygenation performed prior to endotracheal suctioning?

options.A: To stimulate the cough reflex in sedated patients
options.B: To dilate the bronchioles for easier passage
options.C: To prevent suction-induced arterial desaturation
options.D: To liquefy thick bronchial mucus plugs
